title: One Piece Chapter 1197: Release date & major spoilers
summary: Discover when One Piece Chapter 1197 will be released as all the major spoilers are revealed.
details: Trending Modern Warfare 4 Twitch EA FC 27 Wardogs GTA 6 TV & Movies Anime One Piece Chapter 1197: Release date & major spoilers by Anamika Das Published: Oct 28, 2026, 15:26 Save for later Save for later Fuji Television Add as a preferred source on Google Follow on Google News One Piece Chapter 1197 has Sanji overcoming his self-hatred and overpowering his opponent, so here’s when it releases and what to expect. The Straw Hats’ chef is one of the most well-written characters in the series. Throughout the story, we see Sanji risking his life again and again to defeat his foes. His self-sacrificing nature is finally explained in the Whole Cake Island Arc, where we learn of the abuse he endured in his childhood. Article continues after ad Sanji’s tendency to get intentionally hurt is explored again in Chapter 1196 , when he remembers his time in the Kamabokko Kingdom. At that time, Ivankov advised him to love himself before anything else if he really wanted to protect the people he cared about. In One Piece Chapter 1197, Sanji embraces his past hurt and becomes the warrior Luffy needs him to be. This also signals that the Holy Knights’ time on Elbaf is about to be over. Article continues after ad Article continues after ad One Piece Chapter 1197 release date and time One Piece Chapter 1197 will be released on Sunday, November 1, 2026, at 7am PT . You can read the latest chapter for free on Manga Plus and find out its global release time zones below: 11am Eastern Time 4pm British Time 5pm European Time 8:30pm Indian Time 11pm Philippine Time One Piece Chapter 1197 major spoilers Shueisha Titled ‘Love is Defense,’ One Piece Chapter 1197 gives a nod to Ivankov’s advice to Sanji about self-love. The chapter focuses entirely on his fight against Killingham. The chapter starts with Sanji contemplating how his body has carried him through many fights and suffered so much. He realizes that protecting it should be his priority. Flashback panels show key figures in Sanji’s life, including Judge, Zeff, and the opponents he faced. Related One Piece Chapter 1196: Release date & major spoilers One Piece Chapter 1195: Release date & major spoilers One Piece Chapter 1193: Release date & major spoilers Article continues after ad Sanji also realizes that his hatred for his own body came from his childhood. He’s always hated his siblings’ bodies and thought he’d rather die than have a body like theirs. This has led him to deliberately risk his own body over the years. Article continues after ad Sanji understands that ordinary Armament Haki won’t be enough to defeat Killingham. He needs a stronger defense to counter the immortal man. He unleashes a barrage of kicks, irritating Killingham so much that the Holy Knight coats himself with black armor through Omen that can Article continues after ad only be broken with the Conqueror’s Haki. Sanji conjures new flames around his leg that look similar to Ifrit Jambe, but the flames’ aura is more fluid. When he blocks Killingham’s attack with it, the tip of Longinus shatters, and Sanji is thrown away by the impact. As Sanji inspects the flames, he finds that his Armament Haki has reached a new level. He no longer feels pain and can now withstand any attack with ease, as if he’s the one attacking. He may even shatter bullets with them. Article continues after ad He stands up, ready to face Killingham. He thinks about how Zoro should be Luffy’s sword, whereas he’d act as his captain’s shield. Black lightning appears around him, indicating that Sanji has finally unlocked his Conqueror’s Haki. Article continues after ad One Piece Chapter 1197 ends with Sanji unleashing a new attack with his flames and Conqueror’s Haki. It shatters the shaft of Longinus and Killingham’s helmet. The last panel shows the Holy Knight spitting blood. Article continues after ad There’ll be no break next week, meaning One Piece will continue with its usual release schedule. Until the next chapter drops, check out our ranking of the best One Piece villains . title: Japanese government still lists refusing to pay for dates as a form of domestic violence
summary: Once again, there’s a lot of nuance that’s lost in the attempt to be succinct. details: Once again, there’s a lot of nuance that’s lost in the attempt to be succinct . As you can probably guess from its name, the Japanese government’s Gender Equality Bureau isn’t a fan of imbalance in interpersonal relationships. What is surprising to many people, though, is the bureau’s assertion that “not paying for any dating expenses” is committing an act of domestic violence . On its website, the bureau lists four categories of “dating domestic violence.” Examples of “physical violence” are pretty obvious – striking, pulling hair, throwing objects, that sort of thing. “Sexual violence,” the bureau says, includes coerced sex, refusal to use contraception, and nonconsensual naked photography or video recording. “Psychological violence” is described as making insulting or disrespectful remarks, forbidding a romantic partner from seeing their friends, or monitoring their email communications. It’s bureau discussion of “economic violence,” though, that’s been raising some eyebrows online in Japan this week. While one could argue that this is using the word “violence” in its broadest possible sense, most of the examples are things that would be considered wrong under basic common sense/decency, such as not paying back money borrowed from a romantic partner, taking money from their bank account without permission, and forbidding them to work outside the home or forcing them to quit their job. But then there’s this example of economic violence: “Not paying for any dating expenses.” Japan may not have a reputation for being the most chivalrous society, and going Dutch, or warikan , as it’s called in Japanese, is more common in casual dating here than it is in some other countries. That said, it’s not at all unusual for guys to pay for everything on a date with a girl, and the government of Japan saying that this is a form of domestic violence has been provoking a lot of responses online to a recent Twitter post pointing out the bureau’s stance. “Yeah, it’s practically theft, so it’s obviously a form of domestic abuse.” “Wait, I’ve never made a girl pay on a date, so does that mean that I’ve been subjected to economic violence in the eyes of the government?” “There are a lot of guys who are the victim of this kind of domestic abuse.” “Does this make guys who habitually treat the girl on dates masochists for actively encouraging dating domestic violence?” “Let’s all make sure to properly split the bill, because the government has said that anything other than that is considered economic violence, OK?” “That’ll show all those gold-digger girls who hang out in Tokyo’s Minato Ward.” “This is wonderful for men. I think all us guys are thinking ‘Hey, can’t you pitch in a little?’ but we can’t say it to the girl because we’re trying to look cool.” “Coerced treating is a crime.” “I think they mean it’s wrong for both guys and girls to refuse to pay for dating expenses.” There’s probably at least a little wry humor behind some of those comments, but the last two are the ones that really get to the heart of the matter. As clarified by a spokesperson for the Gender Equality Bureau when this example of economic violence also became a topic of online discussion a few years ago , the bureau recognizes that “Both men and women can be victims of this kind of violence” and that “If both sides are OK with [one person not paying], it’s not domestic violence.” It’s when one person attempts to force their partner to shoulder all of the dating costs against their will that it crosses the line into unacceptable behavior, or when someone demands to be reimbursed for past dating expenses that, at the time, they offered to pay for. ▼ Just like going to a butcher shop on a date is fine if that’s what both you and your sweetheart are into, so too is it OK if you’re in agreement that you’ll be treating her to a half-kilo of ground beef. In other words, the bureau’s guidelines are more about discouraging someone from unilaterally declaring “We’re going out, and you’re going to pay for me” or becoming verbally abusive if asked to chip in, not shaming someone for consistently accepting offers to be treated . But while we’re on the subject of “other words,” as mentioned above, this is not the first time the vague language used on the bureau’s website regarding who pays on a date has caused confusion, and the list of examples being followed by the declaration that “All of these are violence” leaves the door open to misinterpretation that context and a couple’s specific circumstances are irrelevant. The statement has remained on the site in its current form since 2018, so maybe it’s time for an update that puts a finer point on things. title: Starbucks Japan releases “Let’s Par-TEA!” Frappuccino and drinks for the holiday season
summary: Each beverage has its own unique character so you can choose which one you’d like to party with. With the holiday season fast approaching, Starbucks is bringing the party spirit to its stores in Japan with a trio of new drinks based around the theme of “Let’s par-TEA!” As the name suggests, the three new holiday […]
details: Each beverage has its own unique character so you can choose which one you’d like to party with. With the holiday season fast approaching, Starbucks is bringing the party spirit to its stores in Japan with a trio of new drinks based around the theme of “ Let’s par-TEA! ” As the name suggests, the three new holiday drinks shine a spotlight on tea, with strawberry , royal milk tea and Earl Grey chocolate featuring in the beverages. The three stars of this tea party each have their own distinct character, so you can choose the one that best suits your mood. Those wanting an elegant pick-me-up can opt for the Joyful Medley Strawberry Creamy Tea Latte , which combines robust black tea with the smooth sweetness of oolong tea and the floral fragrance of jasmine tea, finished with a subtle hint of apricot. ▼ Joyful Medley Strawberry Creamy Tea Latte (Tall size only, 638 yen [US$4.03] for takeout; 650 yen for dine-in) The blended tea base is joined by sweetened fresh cream and a topping of strawberry-flavoured mousse and freeze-dried strawberries. The rich aroma of the chain’s famous Joyful Medley blend, which is reminiscent of apricot jam, is layered with creamy sweetness, while the finish remains refreshing, allowing you to enjoy a variety of tastes and aromas throughout the beverage. ▼ Earl Grey Chocolate Frappuccino (Tall size only, 678 yen takeout; 690 yen dine-in) Those wanting a little more playfulness can reward themselves with this tea-and-chocolate Frappuccino, which combines aromatic Earl Grey with rich chocolate sauce and crunchy chocolate chips. It has a mellow, layered flavour, with the gentle fragrance of bergamot and the taste of black tea spreading through the palate with every sip, while the chocolate chips add crunchy textural contrast, capturing the playful spirit of the holiday season. ▼ Royal Milk Tea (609 yen takeout; 620 yen dine-in) Finally, we have a rich, blended milk tea that combines milk with an original blend of three teas: Darjeeling , Assam and Ceylon . The full-bodied flavour of the tea harmonises with the mellow creaminess of the milk, creating a rich and rewarding taste that tea lovers will fall in love with. As an extra special holiday treat, Starbucks is also adding a cookie option, so you can add more flavour and a dash of cuteness to any iced beverage that’s topped with whipped cream or mousse foam. ▼ Be a Santa Cookie Topping (69 yen takeout; 70 yen dine-in) The “Be a Santa Cookie Topping” has a buttery aroma and crisp yet crumbly shortbread texture. The three designs – a present, a Christmas tree and a Santa hat – are provided at random so, like a Christmas present, you won’t know what you’re getting until it’s given to you by the barista. While the cookie topping will be available while stocks last from 2-19 November, the drinks will be on the menu for a limited (but unspecified) time from 2 November. title: Shinkansen online ticketing service reports customer data leak
summary: Online reservation system handles tickets for Shinkansen’s “Golden Route” and Kyushu. If you’re planning to take a ride on the Shinkansen, the Smart EX online ticketing service is a handy utility. Managed by Shinkansen operator Central Japan Railway Company/JR Central, Smart EX lets you book seats on bullet trains running in eastern and western Japan, […]
details: Online reservation system handles tickets for Shinkansen’s “Golden Route” and Kyushu . If you’re planning to take a ride on the Shinkansen , the Smart EX online ticketing service is a handy utility. Managed by Shinkansen operator Central Japan Railway Company/JR Central , Smart EX lets you book seats on bullet trains running in eastern and western Japan, as well as the southwestern island of Kyushu. A wide selection of credit cards can be used for payment, and the Smart EX mobile app can provide you with a QR code so that you don’t have to fuss around with a paper ticket. Unfortunately, it’s not just travelers that have found Smart EX alluring, but hackers too, as JR Central has announced a data breach has resulted in personal information of roughly 170,000 Smart EX users being leaked . The incident stems from another security breach earlier this month at Yumirulink, a digital marketing and email forwarding service involved in the routing of some Smart EX messages. Thankfully, the Smart EX user data that was stolen is of a limited scope. According to JR Central’s statement, hackers were able to obtain the users’ names, email addresses, member IDs/screen names, and membership types . Date of birth, home addresses, phone numbers, and credit card numbers and expiration dates were not leaked, the company says. In addition, JR Central says that only the renderings of users’ names in Japanese katakana phonetic characters were leaked, and other forms were not compromised. However, it’s somewhat unclear if this assertion applies only to non-katakana Japanese text (i.e. kanji-character) versions of user names, or if it also is meant to cover names written in the Latin alphabet, since as of this writing the Smart EX website only has a statement regarding the data leak on its Japanese-language page, with no mention of it on the service’s English site. JR Central’s statement also says that the data breach was not connected to auto-generated emails such as those that Smart EX sends to confirm bookings or customer-initiated schedule changes, and instead is related to emails sent for things such as sale promotions or altered timetable notifications following the recent Kumamoto earthquake. Collectively, the Smart EX system covers Shinkansen bookings for bullet trains operated by JR Central, JR West, and JR Kyushu , which together stretch from Tokyo through Osaka, Kyoto, and Hiroshima on to Fukuoka and then down to Kagoshima. So if you’ve used the service to book a Shinkansen ticket along that network, it’s probably a good idea to keep an eye on your various other online accounts in the coming days, just in case someone out there has some of your personal data. title: Japan’s super cute tanuki bread skips tricks, promises to be treat for your eyes and taste buds
summary: You can trust this tanuki to be as sweet on the inside as it looks on the outside. In Japanese folklore, tanuki are tricksters. There’s nothing they love more than playing pranks on us unsuspecting humans, and that image of them even extends to Japanese cuisine. “Tanuki soba” and “tanuki udon” are styles of noodles […]
details: You can trust this tanuki to be as sweet on the inside as it looks on the outside . In Japanese folklore, tanuki are tricksters. There’s nothing they love more than playing pranks on us unsuspecting humans, and that image of them even extends to Japanese cuisine. “Tanuki soba” and “tanuki udon” are styles of noodles topped with tempura flakes only, because those crafty racoon dogs have tricked you by already eating the shrimp or veggies that would ordinarily be inside the tempura. But at the same time, tanuki are really, really cute, and thankfully it’s this aspect that Japanese bakery Kimuraya has chosen to focus on for the treats that’ll be coming out of their ovens next month. Called Tanuki-kun (-kun being a form of address in Japanese that’s friendlier and more familiar than -san), these baked goods are the polar opposite from tanuki soba/udon in terms of filling generosity. Inside the bun is a mixture of caramel cream and chocolate chips , promising a richly sweet and satisfying flavor profile with an interesting texture too. On the outside, the tanuki’s facial features are made of chocolate, and the mask-like marking around its eyes, and part of its ears too, are rendered with a chocolate biscuit dough . Kimuraya is a little on the premium-priced side for a Japanese bakery, and the 400-yen (US$2.50) Tanuki-kun is likewise a little more expensive than the average bakery treat, but with something that looks this delicious and adorable, we can make room in our snack budget. The Tanuki-kun goes on sale at Kimuraya bakeries from November 1, but can also be ordered through the Kimuraya online store as of October 28 . Red, green, white and gold are the main colours in the collection, with Bearistas and ribbons adding an extra touch of cuteness and glamour to the festivities. title: Cup Noodle launching “isekai” crossover line featuring flavors from outside instant ramen world
summary: An isekai trip for your taste buds, no truck accident required. Isekai translates to “alternate world,” but within the Japanese pop culture sphere it’s also the name of a genre of anime, novels, and other media in which someone gets transported from our mundane plane of existence to a realm with new adventures waiting for […]
details: An isekai trip for your taste buds, no truck accident required . Isekai translates to “alternate world,” but within the Japanese pop culture sphere it’s also the name of a genre of anime, novels, and other media in which someone gets transported from our mundane plane of existence to a realm with new adventures waiting for them. A salaryman might be whisked away to a second life as a spacefaring explorer, or a schoolgirl might awaken to find herself reborn in a kingdom where she’s now part of a web of romantic courtly intrigue. But now it’s Cup Noodles’ turn to get isekai-ed, as Nissin has announced three new flavors that combine their instant noodles with other beloved food brands from outside the cup ramen world. First up for the Cup Noodle Isekai Gattai series ( gattai meaning “combination”) is a collaboration between the standard Cup Noodle flavor and Gindaco , one of Japan’s most popular takoyaki (octopus ball) chains. The familiar Cup Noodle broth gets enhancements of extra dashi (bonito stock), and the customary takoyaki ingredients of powdered seaweed, pickled ginger, plus flavors evocative of the sweet sauce that’s squirted on the dumplings . Inside the cup, Cup Noodle’s iconic “mystery meat” is joined by the similarly mysterious-sounding “octopus-style balls.” There’s also an extra packet of oil on the side to add after the noodles cook as a salute to the oil that Gindako adds to its takoyaki. Next up is a meeting of the worlds of Curry Cup noodle and Karamucho , Japan’s spiciest mass-market crisp potato stick snacks. The already piquant curry broth gets its heat turned up a notch with the addition of chilies , plus garlic too. Floating in that spicy/savory mix are pieces of chili-spiced potato , mystery meat, and carrots. And finally, Seafood Cup Noodle joins forces with Gohan Desu Yo , a brand of simmered seaweed. Gohan Desu Yo is usually eaten by adding a small spoonful to a bowl of white rice, but for this team-up you get a packet of simmered seaweed paste to squeeze into the broth after cooking. That broth is based on the Seafood Cup Noodle, but with extra seaweed, and the oceanic theme continues with pieces of squid and imitation crab, plus cabbage, egg, and green onion. All three varieties are priced at 259 yen (US$1.65) scheduled to go on sale November 9 . title: Japanese snack lovers may soon be spore-ting the latest crowdfunded confectionery tech
summary: Play that fung-ky music. From creepy penguins hatching from eggs to flying balls of chaos, Japan likes to jump on the latest quirky trends, and if history is anything to go by, people will soon be putting fungi in their ears. If you have ever browsed the snack aisle of a Japanese convenience store, there’s […]
details: Play that fung-ky music. From creepy penguins hatching from eggs to flying balls of chaos , Japan likes to jump on the latest quirky trends, and if history is anything to go by, people will soon be putting fungi in their ears . If you have ever browsed the snack aisle of a Japanese convenience store, there’s a chance that you might have encountered Kinoko no Yama , bite-sized treats consisting of a crunchy biscuit stem topped with a chocolate mushroom cap. Now, imagine putting one in your ear. Rather than being the latest dietary trend, or attempting to commune deeper with nature through the chocolate mycelia, what appears to be the start of a fungal colony growing out of your head is in fact the second-generation Kinoko no Yama Wireless Earphones Pro , a tech accessory that looks like you’re using actual confectionery as audio equipment. The concept originally started as a playful visual joke on social media, but after an overwhelming response from netizens demanding to know where they could buy a pair, Kagomedia collaborated with Kinoko no Yama’s maker Meiji to turn them into a reality. The first batch of 3,500 units launched on the Japanese crowdfunding platform Makuake in early 2024 and famously sold out in a shocking ten minutes . ▼ Achieving 9,836 percent of its one million yen goal. Two and a half years later, these chocolate earbuds are making a comeback from November 1 , with a new revival project for the updated 2027 Pro model . If the campaign sees at least 1,000 people pledge that they want a pair, the second generation will officially go into production, but this time they will be made-to-order without a strict limit on quantities , so all those who want will be able to get their hands and ears on them. Despite looking like a novelty gimmick, these earbuds pack some serious tech, with upgraded audio tuning and gold-plated touch sensors. The most ambitious feature though is the built-in AI simultaneous translation covering 144 global languages and dialects . So while you might look like you’re trying to store your snacks in your ears for later to onlookers, you could be able to understand nearly 150 languages in real time. The case itself is designed to mirror the original snack box , complete with a pop-up tray where the two little mushrooms rest inside. If you, like your 3,500 predecessors, want some fungi in your head, you’ll need to check out Makuake on November 1 at 12:00 p.m. , where for the first 24 hours, the first 1,000 pairs of earphones will be sold at the same price as the first-generation (29,800 yen [US$188.96]). The next 2,000 pairs can be bought for 31,800 yen, and the following 2,000 for 33,000 yen. The last possible discount is for 3,000 pairs at 34,800 yen before each unit is sold for its regular price of 36,300 yen with no quantity limits as long as the order is placed before December 13, 2026 , after which you will not be able to purchase these any more. Whether you find the design quirky or strange, it’s a high-quality blend of everyday Japanese pop culture with high-tech innovation, so there’s no need to panic the next time you spot someone on the train with mushrooms sprouting from their ears. title: Japan getting a brand-new batch of Pokémon manhole covers in eastern prefecture this fall
summary: Five new reasons for Pokémon fans to head north from Tokyo. Fall is a fantastic time to take a trip to Gunma Prefecture. Located about two hours north of Tokyo, Gunma gets some beautiful autumn foliage and it also boasts some of east Japan’s finest hot springs, making for a great combo of crisp afternoon […]
details: Five new reasons for Pokémon fans to head north from Tokyo . Fall is a fantastic time to take a trip to Gunma Prefecture . Located about two hours north of Tokyo, Gunma gets some beautiful autumn foliage and it also boasts some of east Japan’s finest hot springs, making for a great combo of crisp afternoon walks followed by a rejuvenatingly warm soak. As of this fall, there’s one more reason to head to Gunma. Well, five actually, as the prefecture is getting five new Pokémon manhole covers! The Pokéfuta/Poké Lids project is a series of artistic one-of-a-kind manhole covers highlighting local communities, helping to draw visitors to lesser-known but still charming parts of Japan. The covers all feature Pocket Monster species and local scenery or representative products such as produce or handicrafts. For example, the Gunma town of Shimonita takes great pride in the quality of the green onions that its farmers grow, so naturally its Pokéfuta, installed in front of the Coconita building next to Shimonita Station, features Farfetch’d, Galarian Farfetch’d, and Sirfetch’d . Boltund naturally feels at home playing in front of Yamba Dam, a towering hydroelectric facility in the town of Naganohara . Joining the Electric-type on this cover, which will be at the Yamba Furusato-kan michi no eki (“road station” local products shop) are Meltan and Seaking , creating further tie-ins with the water/engineering theme. Zigzagoon , in both standard and Galarian forms, appears on the Pokéfuta for the Tsutsujigaoka Fureai Center, located inside Tsutsujigaoka Park in the town of Tatebayashi . This one might actually be best to wait until spring to visit, as tsutsuji is the Japanese word for azalea, and the park contains some 10,000 bushes on which the seasonal flowers bloom. Dunsparce and Shiftry can be seen hanging out on their manhole cover at the entrance to the hiking trail that leads to Fukiware Falls in the town of Numata , placed next to the parking area that hikers can use. Shiftry is here because his design is based on the tengu (crow spirits) of Japanese folklore, who are often depicted using giant leaves or fans to create strong gusts of wind. Tengu are prominently featured in the folklore surrounding Numata’s Miroku Temple on Mt. Kasho, which claims to have the largest tengu mask in all of Japan. And finally, as you board or exit the Shibukawa Ikaho Ropeway at Hototogisu Station in the town of Shibukawa , you’ll be able to say hi to Zapdos , who, being a Flying-type Pokémon, can enjoy expansive views and mountain scenery without having to ride one of the ropeway’s gondolas. ▼ The Pokéfuta locations within Gunma Prefecture All five new Pokémon manhole covers are scheduled to be installed by the end of November . summary: La película recopilatoria de Takopii no Genzai presentó un nuevo tráiler, tema musical y fecha de estreno para cines.
details: Anime La película de Takopii no Genzai revela tráiler y fecha de estreno Tele interpreta el tema principal del filme recopilatorio que llega a los cines en noviembre. Kenji 23 de octubre de 2026 2 Comentarios ADS Si creías que tu estabilidad emocional ya se había recuperado después del trago amargo que nos hizo pasar la adaptación animada, tenemos noticias que te van a revolver el estómago otra vez. El equipo detrás de El Pecado Original de Takopi ( Takopii no Genzai ) presentó un nuevo tráiler y una imagen promocional para su película recopilatoria titulada Takopii no Genzai -Arigatou, Mata Ashita- , confirmando además que llegará a las salas de cine en Japón el próximo 27 de noviembre . Este largometraje se encarga de reestructurar los seis episodios que compusieron la miniserie de televisión, agregando secuencias completamente nuevas para enriquecer la experiencia en la pantalla grande. title: ¿Traducir todo es obligación? Autor de manga contesta a quienes justifican la piratería
summary: El productor de manga Yu Mashiro explicó por qué las editoriales priorizan el mercado japonés y abordó los problemas de la localización.
details: Manga ¿Traducir todo es obligación? Autor de manga contesta a quienes justifican la piratería Yu Mashiro explicó los altos costos de la localización y criticó las malas traducciones. Kenji 24 de octubre de 2026 12 Comentarios ADS Cada vez que un manga no recibe una traducción oficial a los pocos días de su salida, no faltan las voces en internet que justifican la piratería argumentando que las editoriales japonesas ignoran al público internacional. Sin embargo, el productor japonés de manga Yu Mashiro decidió poner las cartas sobre la mesa y explicar sin rodeos por qué publicar un título al otro lado del mundo no es tan sencillo como apretar un botón. El creativo señaló que el manga en Japón se sigue produciendo pensando de forma exclusiva en el público local. Son los números de ventas dentro del territorio japonés los que deciden si una historia continúa en publicación o termina cancelada, por lo que el interés internacional resulta una sorpresa agradable, pero de ningún modo el motor principal del negocio. Para las editoriales, traer una obra a Occidente representa un riesgo financiero real y no una obligación hacia los lectores extranjeros. Mashiro detalló que localizar una obra va muchísimo más allá de cambiar el idioma de los globos de texto. El proceso exige adaptar referencias culturales complicadas de entender fuera de Japón, rediseñar viñetas cuando el formato o la dirección de lectura lo requiere y asumir costos de licencias que, en muchos casos, no logran recuperarse con las ventas en el extranjero. Si las proyecciones financieras no garantizan ganancias aceptables, la inversión simplemente no se aprueba. Por si los costos fueran poco, el productor también criticó los precedentes de malas localizaciones en el mercado de habla inglesa. Como ejemplos, recordó las modificaciones drásticas sufridas por Crayon Shin-chan al intentar americanizar su humor con chistes de la cultura pop occidental, o las alteraciones en la saga Gundam donde se inventaron términos de ciencia ficción ajenos al material original. Asimismo, lamentó aquellos casos donde los propios traductores modifican diálogos para meter visiones o agendas personales, alejándose de la intención real del autor. La industria del manga en Japón opera bajo un modelo fuertemente centralizado en el consumo interno a través de revistas y volúmenes recopilatorios. Aunque el consumo internacional ha crecido durante los últimos años, la estructura comercial de los grandes sellos editoriales prioriza asegurar la rentabilidad en las librerías japonesas antes de comprometer recursos en licencias internacionales. Esta dinámica implica que la enorme mayoría de las historias publicadas en Japón jamás cruzarán la frontera de forma oficial, permaneciendo como títulos exclusivos para el público local a menos que alcancen un nivel de éxito masivo que justifique los riesgos de exportación. ¿Qué opinas sobre las declaraciones de Yu Mashiro y la realidad de las traducciones oficiales? title: Capcom sufre un hackeo masivo y se filtran datos de casi 12 millones de cuentas
summary: Capcom confirmó un ciberataque a su servicio Capcom ID que afectó a más de 11.7 millones de registros de usuarios.
details: VideoJuegos Capcom sufre un hackeo masivo y se filtran datos de casi 12 millones de cuentas La empresa notificó a la policía japonesa tras detectar el acceso no autorizado a su sistema. Meta Title Yuna 23 de octubre de 2026 2 Comentarios ADS Si eres de los que tiene una cuenta para jugar en línea con la compañía de Resident Evil y Street Fighter , más vale que le eches un ojo a tu correo. La desarrolladora japonesa Capcom confirmó que sufrió un serio incidente de seguridad en su plataforma de usuarios Capcom ID , dejando al descubierto la información de casi doce millones de registros en todo el mundo. La compañía detectó actividad sospechosa en sus servidores el pasado lunes 19 de octubre e inició un protocolo de emergencia para bloquear accesos no autorizados. Tras las investigaciones iniciales, la empresa descubrió que un tercero logró vulnerar la base de datos de su servicio de membresías, afectando a un total de 11,774,247 registros a nivel global. Entre la información comprometida se encuentran direcciones de correo electrónico e identificadores del sistema como la fecha de creación de la cuenta, fecha del último inicio de sesión, cantidad de ingresos y la dirección IP utilizada. A pesar del enorme volumen de datos expuestos, el equipo de ciberseguridad logró contener los daños más graves. De todas las cuentas afectadas, la intrusión logró alterar las contraseñas de 196 usuarios de forma no autorizada y acceder a datos personales como fecha de nacimiento, género, región y apodo en 43 casos específicos. La buena noticia dentro de este trago amargo es que la empresa no ha confirmado la filtración de las contraseñas originales elegidas por los usuarios y ya procedió a restablecer los accesos de las cuentas vulneradas. Además, aclararon que la información de tarjetas de crédito no sufrió ningún tipo de afectación. Ante la gravedad del asunto, la firma no se quedó de brazos cruzados. Tras formar un comité interno para evaluar el impacto, el miércoles 21 de octubre presentaron la denuncia formal ante la Policía Prefectural de Osaka y la Comisión de Protección de Información Personal de Japón. La desarrolladora habilitó canales de atención al cliente dedicados para este incidente y comenzará a ponerse en contacto con los usuarios afectados mientras implementa nuevas medidas para reforzar la seguridad de su infraestructura digital. Capcom es una de las empresas de videojuegos más importantes e históricas de Japón, fundada en 1983. details: Anime Date A Live F Last Date revela su tráiler oficial y fecha de estreno en cines El estudio Fugaku confirmó que la película final de Date A Live se estrenará en marzo de 2027. Aunque el título de la película y el estudio de animación ya se habían dado a conocer a inicios de este año, no fue sino hasta esta presentación especial donde se hizo oficial que el desenlace llegará a los cines de forma cinematográfica, prometiendo una producción visual impresionante para despedir a Shido y a las espíritus. Sobre Date A Live Date A Live es una exitosa franquicia de novelas ligeras de ciencia ficción, comedia romántica y fantasía escrita por Koushi Tachibana e ilustrada por Tsunako . La obra impresa comenzó su publicación en marzo de 2011 bajo el sello Fantasia Bunko de Kadokawa, concluyendo en marzo de 2020 con un total de 22 volúmenes recopilatorios. Su carácter tímido y los constantes “quiero volver a mi cabaña en las montañas” contrastan con los momentos en los que revela todo su talento y valentía. Los lectores destacaron la evolución de Monica: “al inicio parecía incapaz de enfrentarse al mundo, pero capítulo tras capítulo mostró un crecimiento entrañable”. También fue aplaudida la construcción narrativa: “cada detalle de la trama tiene un propósito y la animación del opening transmite belleza y simbolismo”. La trama narra la relación entre Rintaro Tsugumi , un chico de apariencia intimidante pero de corazón noble, y Kaoruko Wakuri , una estudiante de un colegio femenino de élite. Fue un momento de madurez y crecimiento que marcó la diferencia en Fullmetal Alchemist: Brotherhood , convirtiéndose en una de las citas más recordadas del doblaje latino. “¡Ayudar sin que te lo pidan, eso es ser un verdadero héroe!” – Boku no Hero Academia Durante su enfrentamiento con Stain , Deku corrigió a Ida con esta frase que resume el ideal de un héroe. En un contexto en el que su vida estaba en peligro, sus palabras resaltaron la esencia del sacrificio y la empatía, consolidando el camino de Izuku como un auténtico símbolo de justicia. “He comprendido que las circunstancias de nuestro nacimiento no importan.” – Pokémon: La película En Pokémon: La primera película , Mewtwo reflexionó sobre su propia existencia con esta frase inolvidable. La frase reflejó la empatía inquebrantable del protagonista, pero también su firmeza al enfrentarse a figuras de autoridad en defensa de lo justo. “Tener más sufrimientos no te da la razón.” – Jujutsu Kaisen Durante el enfrentamiento contra Mechamaru , Panda pronunció esta reflexión contundente. Reconoció el dolor de su rival, pero dejó en claro que la desgracia personal no justifica acciones que dañan a los demás. Un recordatorio fuerte de que el sufrimiento no es una excusa para la injusticia. “No pierdas el tiempo intentando ser el bueno.” – Bleach En medio de la batalla contra Coyote Starrk , el Capitán Shunsui Kyoraku pronunció esta frase que refleja la crudeza de la guerra. details: Anime El anime Our Last Crusade or the Rise of a New World tendrá una tercera temporada El estudio SILVER LINK. y el reparto principal regresan para dar continuidad a la historia. El anuncio vino acompañado por una primera imagen promocional dibujada por la diseñadora de personajes Kaori Yoshikawa, en la que se aprecia a Iska y Rin preparándose para infiltrarse en el Imperio con el objetivo de rescatar a Sisbell, mientras Aliceliese los observa con evidente preocupación desde la distancia. Para esta nueva etapa, los estudios SILVER LINK. y Studio Palette volverán a unir fuerzas en la producción de animación, manteniendo a Yuki Inaba como director y responsable de la supervisión de los guiones, mientras que Kaori Yoshikawa estará nuevamente a cargo de los diseños de personajes. El reparto de actores de voz principal también se mantendrá intacto para dar continuidad a los personajes. Yusuke Kobayashi regresar en el papel de Iska, acompañado por Sora Amamiya dando vida a la princesa Aliceliese Lou Nebulis IX. El autor de las novelas ligeras, Kei Sazane, dedicó un mensaje de agradecimiento a los seguidores por el constante apoyo, destacando que esta tercera entrega abordará acontecimientos a una escala mucho mayor y revelará secretos fundamentales que van al corazón mismo de la trama. Esta confirmación representa un momento de estabilidad para la franquicia, recordando que la primera temporada se emitió en octubre de 2020, mientras que la segunda temporada atravesó una reestructuración completa en su calendario tras suspender su emisión a mediados de 2024 para garantizar los estándares de calidad visual, reanudando su transmisión desde el primer episodio en abril de 2025. Our Last Crusade or the Rise of a New World es una saga de novelas ligeras de fantasía y ciencia ficción escrita por Kei Sazane e ilustrada por Ao Nekonabe . La obra comenzó a publicarse bajo el sello de la editorial Kadokawa en mayo de 2017, acumulando 16 volúmenes impresos hasta la fecha. Su popularidad dio pie a una adaptación al manga dibujada por Okama en la revista Young Animal a partir de mayo de 2018, la cual se recopiló en siete volúmenes, además de contar con una serie de novelas secundarias tituladas Secret File . La historia nos traslada a un mundo dividido por un prolongado conflicto bélico entre el Imperio, una potencia guiada por un alto desarrollo tecnológico, y la Soberanía de Nebulis, una nación habitada por brujas que dominan la magia astral. El argumento sigue a Iska, el espadachín más joven en ostentar el título de la fuerza suprema del Imperio, y a Aliceliese Lou Nebulis IX, la princesa heredera del bando rival. El actor de voz Masaya Fukunishi , quien interpreta al querido protagonista Kafka Hibino, no pudo ocultar su emoción ante los asistentes y compartió unas palabras muy especiales sobre el cierre de la franquicia. title: El anime Akane-banashi confirma su segunda temporada para enero de 2027
summary: El anime Akane-banashi anunció oficialmente la producción de su segunda temporada para enero de 2027.
details: Anime El anime Akane-banashi confirma su segunda temporada para enero de 2027 El anime adaptara el esperado Arco de Zenza y se estrenara en enero de 2027. En esta nueva etapa, la historia nos adentrará de lleno en el esperado Arco de Zenza, acompañando a Akane Osaki, ahora conocida formalmente bajo el nombre artístico de Akane Arakawa, tras graduarse de la preparatoria e ingresar a la escuela de Shiguma. La joven contadora de historias dará sus primeros pasos profesionales en el tradicional teatro Yasaka-tei, rodeada de verdaderos maestros del género en una competencia narrativa sin igual. Acompañando este anuncio, se reveló un primer avance en vídeo y una imagen promocional enfocada en la nueva etapa de la protagonista. Además, se sumaron nuevos integrantes al elenco de voces, destacando a Taku Yashiro en el papel de Asagao Konjakutei y a Yoji Ueda como Hassho Tsubakiya. Estas voces se unen a las incorporaciones que aparecieron en el cierre de la entrega anterior, entre las que destacan reconocidos actores como Hochu Otsuka como Miroku Kashiwaya, Ryotaro Okiayu como Shomei Tsubakiya, Hiroshi Naka como Enso Sanmeitei, Mutsumi Tamura como Urara Ransaika, Shinichiro Miki como Ryu'un Kenputei y Tomokazu Seki como Chocho Konjakutei. La primera entrega de la serie se emitió entre abril y junio, abarcando hasta la conclusión del emocionante Arco de la Copa Karaku. Aquella producción contó con la dirección de Ayumu Watanabe en el estudio ZEXCS, con Yu Harima como asistente de dirección, Kii Tanaka a cargo del diseño de personajes y la dirección de animación, Michihiro Tsuchiya en la supervisión de los guiones y Akio Izutsu en la composición musical, contando además con la asesoría especializada del maestro Kikuhiko Hayashiya para representar con fidelidad el arte del rakugo. Sobre Akane-banashi Akane-banashi es un aclamado manga escrito por Yuki Suenaga e ilustrado por Takamasa Moue . La obra comenzó su publicación en la famosa revista Weekly Shonen Jump de la editorial Shueisha en febrero de 2022, habiendo lanzado su volumen recopilatorio número 24 el pasado 2 de octubre. Desde su debut, el título se convirtió en una de las mayores sorpresas del catálogo de la revista, cosechando nominaciones a premios prestigiosos como los Kodansha Manga Awards y el Manga Taisho en 2023. title: Beloved, 100-year-old Tokyo public bathhouse Sengenyu is about to get a second life this December
summary: Various entities take a dip together to save a community institution and preserve public bath culture for the next generation to enjoy. details: Various entities take a dip together to save a community institution and preserve public bath culture for the next generation to enjoy. Public bathhouses , known as sento in Japanese, have long served as important community gathering hubs where different generations can interact with one another. Unfortunately, not all public baths are able to stay afloat in this age of rising costs and other factors. Case in point: from 2015 to 2025, the number of public bathhouses operating in Tokyo dropped from 628 to 417 locations. Thankfully, one public bath in Tokyo’s Nerima Ward called Sengenyu is not going to join those statistics anytime soon. First opened in 1927, the third-generation previous owner was on the verge of closing the beloved community staple due to their family’s increasing age and the deteriorating facilities. However, thanks to the Tokyo Public Bathhouse Succession Matching Program offered jointly by the Tokyo Metropolitan Government and the Tokyo Public Bathhouses Association, a new owner in company Ofuro Works was found. Now, instead of being demolished, Sengenyu is currently being renovated and will reopen to the public in early December. ▼ The current exterior of Sengenyu The project includes large-scale remodeling of Sengenyu’s entrance, lobby, changing rooms, and saunas to update certain facilities. ▼ Rendition of the completed exterior, designed to blend in with the surrounding area The lobby is particular is intended to become a spacious, relaxing entryway where patrons can soak in the warmth of the natural wood theme inside. In addition, a new electric heater from Japanese bath company Metos will be installed within the saunas. Patrons can continue to throw water on the rocks themselves in order to increase the steam to their desired level. These new updates don’t mean that Sengenyu will lose all of its original charm, though, as features such as the retro-style bathroom with its colorful tile art and the Shigaraki ware tanuki statue outside will be preserved in its redesign. In a delightful community collaboration, Ofuro Works is also partnering with students at the local Nihon University College of Art to design an updated logo and mascot character based on the tanuki statue. It’s a true full-circle moment, as students from this school as well as other local universities have long been going to Sengenyu and can now leave their own personal mark on the space for many more years to come. Finally, widespread public fundraising efforts are set to begin on November 1 through Japan’s largest crowdfunding site, Campfire . The project aims to raise 1 million yen (US$6,375) to help offset the costs of remodeling and updating the bath facilities. Financial backers will receive a towel, t-shirt, and a sneak-peek of Sengenyu behind the scenes before it reopens for business. ▼ The art students’ new logo combines the steam of a bathhouse with the puff of smoke that occurs when a tanuki transforms in Japanese folklore. Despite the decrease in the total number of Tokyo public bathhouses, we can only hope that the statistics showing that the number of users is actually going up will allow Sengenyu and other bath facilities in the Greater Tokyo Area to flourish for 100 more years and beyond. title: Fishing information website for Susaki, Japan, hit by data leak, all 3 users affected
summary: Personal information for everyone posting to the site over the past year compromised. For the past week, there has been an inordinate number of hacking and data leakage from all kinds of websites, from 6.6 million people’s names, emails, and, in some cases, driver’s license info taken from major car rental and parking service Times […]
details: Personal information for everyone posting to the site over the past year compromised . For the past week, there has been an inordinate number of hacking and data leakage from all kinds of websites, from 6.6 million people’s names, emails, and, in some cases, driver’s license info taken from major car rental and parking service Times to the details of registered users on the Burger King app. With new leaks being reported literally every day, it’s getting to the point where you’d be in the minority to not have been affected somehow. The latest data breach reported has come out of the city of Susaki in Kochi Prefecture . This coastal city with a population of about 20,000 people recently had their municipal fishing information website Tsuri-Baka City Susaki (Fishing-Crazy City Susaki) hacked. It appears that a company in Tokyo that manages the website’s servers was attacked and notified the fishing site on 16 October, causing them to shut down the site while an investigation is carried out. ▼ The entire Fishing-Crazy City Susaki website is down as of this writing. As a result, everyone who used the site’s inquiry form from July 2025 to July 2026 may have had their names, email addresses, phone numbers, and details of their fishing inquiry compromised. According to the fishing bureau’s records, as many as three people may have been affected during this period. The details of the inquiries have not surfaced on the dark web but could range anywhere from how they’re bitin’ on a specific day to recommendations for a good restaurant that’ll clean and cook the day’s catch. The current downtime is also a concern, with as many as one person potentially unable to request fishing information for the area from an official government source as opposed to other reviews on the Internet or just talking to people around town. Online comments expressed a difficulty in facing the full severity of this hack, with some resorting to humor as a defense mechanism. “Wouldn’t it be easier just to apologize to those three people directly? Why tell all us?” “Maybe all the victims can go on a fishing trip together.” “This data breach is on a completely different level from anything we’ve seen before.” “Honestly, it takes guts to come forward and admit this. I respect that.” “I guess that’s a good thing, for some people at least.” “It’s kind of scary that even places like that are getting hit.” “I would like to apply for the job of the person handling their inquiries.” I think the positive spin that can be put on all this is that it’s quite likely only a few people used the inquiry form of Fishing-Crazy City Susaki because it is such a comprehensive website and rich in detail that almost no one reading it would be left with any questions to ask. And by providing such stellar information, they managed to keep the fallout from this server attack to an absolute minimum. It just goes to show that in these times of increasingly tenuous cyber-security, our first line of defense is quality fishing information. title: Is this crazy-looking home sauna just what our busy daddy reporter needs in his life?
summary: Ahiruneko’s single-guy sauna days are done, but this gadget promises to bring the steam right into his home. Back in his bachelor days, our Japanese-language reporter Ahiruneko used to go to a sauna once or twice a week. details: Ahiruneko’s single-guy sauna days are done, but this gadget promises to bring the steam right into his home . Back in his bachelor days, our Japanese-language reporter Ahiruneko used to go to a sauna once or twice a week. Now, though, he’s got a wife and kid , plus an apartment out in the suburbs that’s closer to the mountains than the office , and thus a long commute, leaving him with only enough time for one or two sauna days in an entire year. So in his quest for the optimal sauna/life balance, he decided to purchase a home sauna . Converting an entire room of his home into a sauna facility would be excessive in terms of cost and floorspace, so instead of doing that he went looking for a home sauna kit on Rakuten, where he found an assemble-it-yourself steam sauna kit for 17,780 yen (US$112). All of the components shipped together in a large cardboard box, and Ahiruneko laid them out to see what he’d be working with. Folded up inside that cloth pouch is the material for the sides of the sauna tent, pictured with it in the above photo are a floor mat, piping for the tent’s frame, one device for producing steam, another for dispersing it inside the tent, and a hose to connect them . Also included in the set were a folding chair and one of those rollers that are supposed to stimulate the pressure points on the bottom of your feet to provide various vague wellness benefits. The included instructions were written in less-than-fluent Japanese, but between them and the photos on the Rakuten product page here , Ahiruneko could figure out what he needed to do. He started by removing the tent material from its pouch and assembling the pipe frame . This was a pretty quick and simple process, and before long the tent was standing in the middle of his living room. It almost looks like a giant down vest, with a slot for your neck and also two little slits that you can open if you want to reach your hands outside the tent . There’s also an exterior pocket where you can keep the remote control to turn the steam generator on and off or adjust the temperature. Speaking of the steam generator, it resembles a rice cooker . You fill it with water, and once the liquid gets hot enough to start turning into steam, it gets channeled through the side of the tent by the connecting tube… …and dispersed by the steam box, which you place inside the sauna with yourself. The dimensions of the tent are cozy, but there’s room to spare in which to fit the chair, and laying down the mat before your steam session will help keep your floor from getting damp. OK, with everything assembled, it was time to turn ono the steam generator! Ahiruneko hit the power button…and had no idea what the display said. That blurriness isn’t from Ahiruneko’s camera. His brand-new home sauna’s display was foggy and indistinct, almost like it was censoring itself with a mosaic. Luckily, the control buttons all had legible labels, and the printed instructions had told Ahiruneko that once steam started coming out of the top of the sauna tent, it was ready for him to step in . It took about 20 minutes for the steam to heat up , but when it did, entering the tent turned out to be surprisingly tricky, since the frame has a pair of connected pipes running horizontally across the front. Ahiruneko ended up having to temporarily pull them apart, step inside the tent, and then put them back together. Now that he was finally inside, all he needed to do was zip the front back up… … and settle in for a steam session . If you’re setting one of these up for yourself, you’ll definitely want to give your housemates a heads up beforehand, so that they don’t wander into the room and think you’ve been decapitated, or maybe had your body from the neck down converted into machinery in order to become a sauna cyborg. But as startling as this setup looks when viewed from the outside, it was extremely relaxing for Ahiruneko on the inside . He’d purposely kept his expectations low about how high the temperature could get, but it turned out that the steam filling his home sauna was surprisingly hot. It wasn’t long until his body was sweating steadily, but his head being exposed kept the environment from feeling stifling or even stuffy. In time, though, Ahiruneko started to sweat from his face too, so he unzipped one of the arm holes so he could grab the remote control and turn down the temperature just a bit. He’d actually put a second remote control in the pocket too, the one for his TV, since having his own personal sauna means he can watch whatever he wants while staming. As for negatives, the device that emits steam inside the tent does, understandably, get very hot, so you do need to be conscious of where it’s placed and make sure not to step on it. You also need to wipe down the tent and let it dry before you fold it back up, which adds a little time and hassle to the start-to-finish process. Still, even with some cleaning up to do, Ahiruneko is still coming out ahead, time-wise, by being able to have a sauna session without having to leave his home. He thinks he’ll still probably look for opportunities to treat himself to a trip to a professional sauna when he has the chance, but for those times when his schedule or budget is tight, he’ll be very happy to use this at-home version again. details: Who wowed our reporters the most with sheer friendliness? Our website has been around for quite a while now, and over the years we’ve even had the opportunity to rub shoulders with famous movie stars and musicians from time to time. Considering we’re known for behavior that some may deem “ gross ” or “ indecent ,” it wouldn’t be too shocking if they treated us like the schlubs we admittedly are, but there have been a few who really seemed to shine as genuinely good people. So, our Japanese language writers would now like to take a moment and give credit where credit’s due to the famous people from Japan, as well as famous people from abroad who visited Japan, who really made a positive impact on us . When it comes to celebrity interviews, P.K. Sanjun is usually our frontline reporter. As such, he’s met the likes of Will Smith , Arnold Schwarzenegger , and Tom Holland , to name a few. But here are the people who made the biggest impression on him. ● Chris Pratt I’ve interviewed a lot of Hollywood actors, and they’ve all been really nice. I sort of think you need to be in order to make it out there. But among them, Chris Pratt stood out as a super nice person. When I finished my interview, I was just sitting there feeling awkward, but he took the initiative and said, “Hey! Let’s take a photo together!” It was a god-tier gesture and made me fall in love with the guy. View this post on Instagram ● Maximum the Ryo-kun He’s a very private person. You could even say he’s mysterious, and very artistic too. But he’s also an absolute legend and totally down to earth when you talk to him. So much so that I found myself wondering, “Does a celebrity like this actually exist?” The rest of the band [that he’s in, Maximum the Hormone], were great too. Nao-chan immediately snapped a picture after Ryo-kun shaved my eyebrows. Even though it’d been years since I last interviewed them, Daisuke-kun greeted me with a friendly “Long time no see!” Of course, Ue-chan, who shyly chatted with me about kendama , was wonderful too. In short, Maximum the Hormone aren’t just great because of their music. They’re a class act as well. If I ever get another chance to meet Ryo-kun, I want to ask him why he loves [’80s Japanese rock band] Lindberg so much. View this post on Instagram Mr. Sato ’s been known to do a few interviews in his days as well, including none other than Santa Claus . But what big names managed to out-nice even Ol’ Saint Nick for our star reporter? ● Cunning Takeyama I’ve met the famous Japanese comedian Cunning Takeyama a few times now, and every time his genuine kindness shines through. His work often involves interacting with the general public in TV segments, so he seems to make a conscious effort to make people feel at ease. That gentle, approachable character he shows the moment he meets someone is something that I aspire to emulate as an adult. View this post on Instagram ● Shinichiro Azumi I’ve been invited on his TBS radio show Nichiyo Tengoku a few times. Even though it’s a live broadcast, he went out of his way to look after me because of my lack of experience in this setting. He has a way of completely managing the flow of conversation but never lets it show by drawing stories out of me naturally. It’s the mark of a true professional and made a strong impression on me in the way I could relax and have a natural conversation with him. You don’t often see Yoshio interviewing famous people, unless it involves a money-making scheme , but he’s often behind the camera at these meet-ups and has interacted with plenty of famous people as well. Here’s who made the biggest impact on him. ● Matt Damon I was a photographer at an interview with him during the release of Jason Bourne. He might be a world-famous actor, but he didn’t act like it at all and answered every question from P.K. with sincerity. I’ve been present for a lot of celebrity interviews, but Matt Damon was the nicest of them all. It really took me aback how humble someone of his stature could be. He was just a very cool guy. ● Yumi Adachi I was the photographer when Seiji interviewed her while pretending to be Yngwie Malmsteen . I always thought she had a very elegant fashion sense and way of life, so I was intimidated to meet her, but she turned out to be incredibly friendly and cheerful, exactly like she is on television. While we were standing around waiting, she noticed I had the latest iPhone at the time and said, ‘Wow, it’s got three lenses!” I still have and cherish that phone to this day. ▼ Yumi Adachi and Yngwie Malmsteen (Seiji Nakazawa) The interviews where Seiji Nakazawa pretended to be Yngwie Malmsteen in an effort to join famous people’s musical projects were always dicey ones. They rarely ended up being actual interviews, and the famous people involved would have had every right to chew us out for making a mockery of the whole process. But it’s also a chance for celebrities to really show how easy-going they can be, as Ahironeko recalls. ● Non This was our very first Yngwie project , and I was the photographer. The awkward tension in the air was so thick both for us and the people on her side. None of us really knew what was going on. Considering that, it wouldn’t have been a surprise if she just snapped at us with, “Excuse me… What the hell are you doing?” But she was all smiles the whole time. A true goddess. View this post on Instagram Takashi Furusawa is a newer addition to our staff and hasn’t been to as many interviews as the others. But that doesn’t mean he hasn’t had his own brushes with greatness. ● Miki Narahashi Miki Narahashi is best known as the voice of Misae Nohara in the long-running hit Crayon Shinchan . But for me, she was also my senpai when I was at voice acting school. I still clearly remember how she always looked out for me, giving me advice and kind encouragement when I had problems. It was a true honor to have studied under her for two years, and I still cherish that experience to this day. ▼ Narar

title: This Tokyo snack shop can send your taste buds on a trip around Japan for just 1,000 yen
summary: There’s a new sweets curator in downtown Tokyo. In an ideal world, we’d spend every single day on a meandering journey through Japan, stopping see the sights and sample the delicacies whenever and wherever the mood struck us. Unfortunately, we don’t have the copious amounts of money or free time that such a lifestyle would […]
details: There’s a new sweets curator in downtown Tokyo . In an ideal world, we’d spend every single day on a meandering journey through Japan, stopping see the sights and sample the delicacies whenever and wherever the mood struck us. Unfortunately, we don’t have the copious amounts of money or free time that such a lifestyle would require, but there is a way to send your taste buds on a trip across Japan for a very affordable price, as we found out on a recent visit to the Marui Annex department store in downtown Tokyo’s Shinjuku neighborhood. On the first floor of the building you’ll find a shop named Edited Japan Shinjuku , which just opened in September . “Edited” isn’t being used with the meaning of revising or altering something, though, but more in the sense of an “editor’s selection,” as Edited Japan is a curator of Japanese regional sweet and salty snacks. The store is stocked with over 100 different items, representing all of Japan’s prefectures , and unlike some food souvenir shops that only offer large-quantity boxes, Edited Japan specializes in individual-serving sizes, letting you pick out a variety of treats without making any major commitment as you search for a new favorite. Another cool thing about Edited Japan is the store’s focus on snacks that are a genuine part of everyday life in their local communities . You won’t find anything that’ll win you brownie points with a snooty coworker or snobby classmate here. Instead, the shelves are filled with things that present a combination of high quality and reasonable price. Think more “This is something people in Kyoto would munch on if they want something sweet on a Sunday afternoon” than “Bring this to the next party you’re invited to so you can show off your refined sensibilities.” So we decided to see how many prefectures’ treats we could taste with a budget of 1,000 yen (US$6.30), and we mean a hard limit of 1,000 – not a single yen more. Thankfully, this still gave us plenty of room to work with, since most of Edited Japan’s items are somewhere in the 100-200 yen range . We had to do some mid-shopping calculations to make sure we didn’t go over, but in the end, we were able to put together a bundle of snacks from six different prefectures, with the total coming to 995 yen . So what did we get? Let’s start at the north of the country, and work our way down, which makes our first entry on the list Hokkaido Dining Kitchen’s Corn Soup (130 yen), from Hokkaido Prefecture . Soup may not be counted as a “snack” in some cultures, but certain varieties in Japan do sort of get treated that way. Corn pottage, for example, is commonly seen as something that’s tasty and moderately filling even when it’s not served as part of a meal, which is why you’ll often see cans of corn soup for sale in Japanese vending machines during the fall and winter. This powdered corn pottage mix, though, is tastier than what you can get from a can, as it’s made with an especially sweet variety of Hokkaido-grown corn and contains no artificial flavors or preservatives . Next have Dutch Senbei rice crackers, from Yamagata Prefecture’s Sakata Beika , which were the value all-star of our shopping trip, priced at just 45 yen. This brand of rice cracker has been a big hit in Yamagata since 1962, but what makes them “Dutch,” other than the cap that person is wearing in wrapper illustration? There are two theories, one of which is that the distinct bumpy texture of the crackers is said to resemble the footprints left by visitors from Japan to the Netherlands, some of the first foreigners to set foot on Japanese soil back in the feudal era, and thus some of the first people to be seen walking around in Western footwear, which was much bulkier than the straw sandals that were the norm for Japanese people at the time. The other possible explanation is that Oranda , the Japanese word for both Holland and Dutch, sounds similar to orada , a way of saying “we” in the Yamagata dialect, which would make “Oranda Senbei” (as the snack is called in Japanese) sound similar to saying something like “the rice crackers we made.” Regardless of why they’re called that, though, Sakata Beika’s Dutch Senbei are crisp and refreshing, lightly salted to enhance, but not replace, the natural flavors of the non-glutinous Yamagata-grown rice that they’re made with. Next we move on to Kyoto , which means it’s time for nama yatsuhashi . Nama yatsuhashi is a folded triangle of soft mochi with a dollop of anko (sweet red bean paste) inside. Chewy and sweet, with just a touch of sophistication from a dusting of cinnamon , nama yatsuhashi are so popular with Kyoto residents and visitors that there are a few different companies that make them. Nishio , who makes the 250-yen matcha -flavored version we picked up, is one of the most respected, because if your company has been around since 1689, you’ve earned a lot of trust. Since nama yatsuhashi’s simple ingredient list lends itself well to experimentation, most makers, Nishio included, have a cycle of seasonal flavors that are only offered at certain times of year, but the matcha ones are so well loved that they’re available pretty much all the time, as long as the day’s stock isn’t sold out. Continuing west, our taste buds arrive in Hyogo Prefecture , where the coastal town of Akashi brings in some of the country’s most delicious octopus, inspiring rice cracker maker Eirakudo to make Akashi Takosen senbei (250 yen). These deep-fried senbei are made with Akashi octopus and treated with a savory, slightly sweet sauce , and they’re just as suited for a midday snack as they are for a pairing with a nice cold beer after work. We shift back into sweets mode as we reach Hiroshima Prefecture , which, like Kyoto, has a particular dessert that’s overwhelmingly associated with it: the momiji manju . Hiroshima Prefecture is famous for its beautiful maples, called momiji in Japanese, and these manju (sweet dumplings) are shaped like the trees’ leaves. The outside

details: Mochido or Mochidon’t. There is no Mochitri . Earlier this year, we stumbled upon a pair of donuts sold by convenience store chain Lawson that completely redefined the genre of convenience store donuts. They were called Mochibee ( Mo-chee-bay ), and came in powdered sugar and roasted soybean (kinako) flavors. Though they tasted delectably sweet, the whole experience was a bittersweet one because this was just a limited trial run, and Mochibee weren’t sold nationwide. But our writer Natsuno Futon was delighted to hear that Lawson have finally gotten their act together and re-released these treats all over Japan, starting on 20 October. However, the name has changed to Mochido , perhaps because the “beh” part of the name led people to think they were bagels instead of the similarly shaped donuts. Hoping only the name was different, she hurried to her nearest Lawson on the evening of the 20th, only to find they were already sold out. Unsure if they were really that popular already or if her timing was just unlucky, she decided to give up for the night but was able to find them the next morning. The same flavors of sugar and kinako were there, and Futon picked up one of each. The price was just the same as before: 171 yen (US$1.10) each. At a glance, they looked exactly the same as she remembered them, with their slightly irregular shape a testament to their chewy fluffiness and a gracious coating of sweet powders. Futon decided to start with the plain sugar , and after cutting off a piece, it seemed to have that same layered texture as before. She reminisced about that delightfully crisp surface, enhanced with cracker flour and poppy seeds. Unable to hold out any longer, she popped a piece into her mouth and was immediately transported back to that blissful afternoon snack last March. It was every bit as good as it was back then, possibly even better somehow. Next, she tried out the kinako flavor . Obviously, the texture was just as good here, but what really knocked it out of the park for this one was the perfect balance of kinako that made its presence known but didn’t overpower the innate deliciousness of the donut itself. Both donuts had incredible attention to detail and seemed more like the kind you’d buy from a bakery rather than a convenience store. Futon was overjoyed after thinking she’d lost these treats forever after the last time. However, she also crunched the numbers, and the calorie intake from these two decadent donuts far outweighed the calories burned during her 30-minute walk to and from the store. This imbalance would not bode well for her waistline, but thus is the life of a donut lover . Photos ©SoraNews24 ● Want to hear about SoraNews24’s latest articles as soon as they’re published? details: Chainsaw-wielding robots prove they can contribute to human mobility in ways other than people running away from them in terror . Japan’s rail network is famous for its sterling safety and reliability records, and neither of those would be achievable without a whole lot of preventive maintenance. East Japan Railway Company (a.k.a. JR East ), one of the nation’s largest rail operators, is constantly monitoring the condition of its tracks and carriages in order to spot potential problems before they occur, and when it spots an issue that needs to be addressed, it dispatches a crew to take care of it. And sometimes some of the members of those crews are chainsaw-wielding robots . JR East’s maintenance division had noticed that tree branches growing over the tracks near Nobeyama Station in Nagano Prefecture needed to be cut and cleared away, in order to keep them out of the way of trains traveling on this section of the Koumi line. To do so, they rolled out one of their new multifunction heavy railway machines, a humanoid robot attached to a vehicle capable of traveling on rails like a train or on streets like a truck . The robot’s left hand is a multi-pronged claw, suited for grabbing and moving branches and other debris, but where things get really awesome is the right hand, which is a chainsaw. The robots appear to be updated versions of the units JR West started using in 2024 . JR East began adding the robots seen in the above videos to its maintenance fleet in March of this year, but there have only been limited opportunities for the public to see them. The company has traditionally tried to schedule its maintenance projects for the middle of the night, so that they can be completed in the time between the last train of the night and the first of the morning, so as not to disrupt service for passengers. An increasing number of maintenance workers have been requesting day shifts, though, and the company is looking to accommodate them, which also affects the robots’ usage, since the machines are human-operated. Online reactions to the JR East robot’s day at Nobeyama have included: “All of a sudden, we’ve got the kind of awesome robots I’ve always dreamed about.” “Yes! It’s so cool how the left and right arms are different.” “Total R-O-B-O-T vibes.” “It reminds me of the robot from [Studio Ghibli’s] Laputa.” “Is this the robot that the T-800 Terminator is gonna get developed from?” “So should we call this a ‘labor,’ like they call the mecha in the Patlabor anime?” “Hey, didn’t I see that thing in Contra: Hard Corps’ train stage?” “It’s a robot, but it’s also kind of cute.” JR East says that shifting a greater number of maintenance projects to daylight hours will necessitate more frequent closures of line during their regular operating hours, but hopes that passengers will be understanding, and acceptance will most likely be easier to accept if they come with the promise of more chances to see robots in action. title: 93-year-old Japanese grannie helps set trap for scam artist half her age
summary: This woman was the target of a criminal scheme, but she definitely wasn’t going the be the victim of it. details: This woman was the target of a criminal scheme, but she definitely wasn’t going the be the victim of it . Over the past few weeks, Japan has seen a sharp spike in the number of data leaks and cyberattacks, with many organizations warning citizens that their personal information may have been compromised. So on October 21, when a 93-year-old woman living in the town of Aisho, Shiga Prefecture , received a phone call from a man informing her that he was a police officer, and that there had been an unauthorized withdrawal of funds from her back account, it was cause for concern. He did assure her, though, that because the problem had been detected quickly, they could remedy it in a swift manner too. The police would need her help to do so, though. First, he instructed her to freeze her bank account. Second, he said that the authorities would need to examine her ATM card, but to make that part of the process as convenient as possible for her, he said that he could send an investigator to pick the card up at her home . Finalizing that pickup time took a little extra conversation, with the woman talking to the man on the phone the next day as well, but eventually they agreed that the investigator would come that very day, October 22, to take come get the card. Now, there are a number of warning lights that might be going off in your head right now. For starters, if there’s been some kind of anomaly with your bank account, it’s usually your bank that will contact you, not the police. Your bank will probably want to be part of the conversation too if you need to relinquish possession of your ATM card, and it’s also sort of unusual for the police to do house calls to pick up evidence rather than asking you to come down to the station. So it’s pretty clear that the woman was the target of scammers . Unfortunately, this sort of scheme, taking advantage of senior citizens’ trusting nature and confusion regarding technology and bureaucracy, is a time-tested, reliable way of defrauding them, and the 47-year-old man who came to pick up the her ATM card was probably feeling smugly satisfied from proving his superior intellect compared to the befuddled woman. However, the woman turned out to be far savvier than the fraudster had bargained for. She hadn’t been sitting in her living room wringing her hands between phone calls. She’d sniffed out that this was a scam, so she got in touch with the nearby Higashiomi Precinct of the Shiga Prefectural Police . She then pretended to have been fooled , but when the man pretending to be a police officer came to her house, there was a squad of real police officers already there, lying in wait, and instead of getting the woman’s ATM card, the man got arrested . As he hasn’t entered a plea or gone to trial, yet, currently his arrest is for “suspicion of attempted fraud.” Honestly, though, of you show up at the door of an elderly woman who’s never met you before and tell her she needs to give you her ATM card, the only possible explanation other than fraud would be if you were robbing her, so things aren’t looking good for him from a legal standpoint either way. It’s unclear whether the man who came to the woman’s home is the same man who’d called her on the phone, but police (the real police) believe that he was working with other criminals to set up the scam, so hopefully they’ll be apprehended as well, perhaps with the help of an equally large network of tough-as-nails grannies.
