title: Japan’s mission to Martian moon and back underway
summary: This mission is expected to be the first-ever Martian moon landing. At 4:41 a.m. on 20 October, an H3 rocket took off from the Tanegashima Space Center in Kagoshima Prefecture. It was carrying the MMX (Martian Moons eXploration), one of Japan’s largest-ever spacecraft, with a weight of 4,480 kilograms (9,877 pounds), and as of this […]
details: This mission is expected to be the first-ever Martian moon landing . At 4:41 a.m. on 20 October, an H3 rocket took off from the Tanegashima Space Center in Kagoshima Prefecture. It was carrying the MMX (Martian Moons eXploration), one of Japan’s largest-ever spacecraft, with a weight of 4,480 kilograms (9,877 pounds), and as of this writing, all systems are operating normally. ▼ And was there ever any doubt that there’s also a cute mascot version of MMX? The MMX’s mission is to travel to Phobos, one of Mars’ moons, land there, pick up samples, and bring them back to Earth. It’s one of the most ambitious Mars missions to date, but Japan’s space agency JAXA has already made a name for itself by landing on asteroids and returning samples successfully on two previous endeavors. Considering Phobos is up to ten times the size of those asteroids and locked into Mars’ orbit, this might seem like an easier mission. However, the key factor is overcoming the gravity of both Phobos and Mars. The MMX will have to make a soft landing on Phobos, then take off again in order to return to Earth. As a result, about 68 percent of the spacecraft’s total weight is just propellant. It is hoped that by collecting material on Phobos, we can learn more about how it and Mars’ other moon, Deimos, were formed. The two leading theories are that they were once asteroids that got captured by Mars’ gravity or that they formed from the debris expelled by a massive collision of something with the red planet. In addition, it is said that about 0.1 percent of material on Phobos is actually Martian soil , having been ejected when meteorites struck the planet. The goal of the MMX is to pick up at least 10 grams of material from Phobos for an estimated 0.01 grams of actual Martian material. ▼ Here’s a simulation of how it should all go down in a nutshell. Whether this will be the first sample from Mars transported by humans back to Earth remains to be seen, however. China is currently preparing to send its Tianwen-3 to Mars, where it will collect 500 grams of pure Martian soil and bring it back to Earth. Both projects are scheduled to return here in 2031, so if everything goes as planned for everyone, it’ll be a relative photo-finish to see which country will be the first to break off a piece of Mars and carry it back. Going according to plan is a big “if” as well. The MMX was originally expected to launch in 2024, but development of the H3 was delayed and the very tight window when Earth and Mars are properly aligned once every two years closed. China will also need to make sure everything progresses like clockwork from now until their launch in 2028 to avoid their own two-year delay. Regardless of whoever does get back first, these samples will help to blow open our understanding of the Martian environment, including the possibility that life once or even still exists there in some form. Then, maybe we can finally get back to checking out our neglected other neighbor Venus someday. It’d be pretty funny if all this time there actually were a bunch of aliens living in those boiling sulphuric clouds, wondering why no one ever comes looking for them. title: Middle Eastern juice bar B-Fresh lands in Harajuku

details: Refresh yourself with fruity sweetness while the crowds have yet to discover the store. Japan’s cafe culture is a flourishing landscape of specialty roasters, themed cafes , and retro junkisssa coffeehouses . However, the presence of large foreign players, led by companies like Starbucks and Gong Cha, can’t be understated due to their expanding presence in the sector. Recently, a budget, large-capacity coffee brand from South Korea, Fave Coffee, has been opening locations one after another, while the world’s largest food and beverage chain Mixue from China is also steadily increasing its number of stores. In this environment, B-Fresh , billing itself as “a brand from the Middle East ,” has made its first splash into the waters of the Japanese market with opening a store in Tokyo’s Harajuku neighborhood on October 1 . Our ace reporter Mr. Sato was slightly worried it would already be bearing the brunt of the throngs of young people that flow through Harajuku’s streets, he still decided to give it a go. About three weeks after the opening of the store, Mr. Sato stepped foot into Harajuku, and despite it being a weekday, Takeshita Street was crowded as usual, with places like Marion Crepes seeing no drop in customers regardless of day or time, with people lining up endlessly. Scouring the streets, Mr. Sato was sure that he was in the right area and was keeping an eye out for one of these telltale lines, indicating a store’s popularity, but it turns out there was no line for B-Fresh at all. This meant great convenience for Mr. Sato, but he lamented the fact that it had just opened and felt kind of desolate already. It may just be that word of mouth for the store hasn’t spread yet, and business will pick up in the weeks to come. On top of that, it looked as if the building is undergoing exterior wall construction , so if there hadn’t been a sign indicating they were open as usual ( tsujodori eigyochu , 通常通り営業中), an uninformed passerby might assume they were not open at all. The store itself is a juice bar that serves smoothies using fresh fruit, acai bowls, and yogurt , with a variety of items that Mr. Sato was unfamiliar with or unsure how to choose. Using the ticket vending machine inside the store, Mr. Sato chose based on appearance and ordered something called B-Pink Brûlée , priced at 1,100 yen (US$7)] for a large (please note that only cashless payments are accepted in the store). While waiting for his order, Mr. Sato inspected the menu some more. The products seem to be broadly divided into three categories: bubble drinks, smoothies, and acai bowls and frozen yogurt . The main representative of the bubble drinks is the Bubble Tea, and you can also choose fruit juice-filled pearls. For smoothies, there are drinks that blend things like Nutella and Oreos along with fruit, and toppings such as superfoods like chia and flaxseed can be added to any order. The range of customization really is quite wide. In light of the numerous options and indecisiveness, Mr. Sato focused on which menu photos looked appealing, but seeing the actual drink itself, he was confident that his choice was not wrong as it looked incredibly delicious. ▼ Plenty of whipped cream and strawberry crunch on top Making up the drink was a mix of strawberries, vanilla milk, and “creme brulee ,” but even after drinking it, Mr. Sato wasn’t quite sure what the creme brulee was actually represented by—he believes it might be the custard cream. The menu photo also showed strawberry pearls inside of it, but that was an additional topping for 100 yen, so Mr. Sato passed on it this time. Even without the additional pops of fruit, it was deliciously sweet. Amid the unseasonably hot weather and a feeling of fatigue after his morning pole dancing practice, the flavor was very refreshing. In the end, it remains to be seen whether or not this brand can catch on in Japan, but for now, it appears that crowds are yet to form. details: Pikachu Sweets bakes up new treats to celebrate Pokémon’s 30th birthday . This year marks the 30th anniversary of Pokémon , which is another way of saying it’s the franchise’s 30th birthday…and everyone knows you can’t celebrate a birthday without cake, right? And if you’re looking for a cake to celebrate this particular birthday, there’s no more appropriate choice than a Pikachu cake . That’s exactly what’s coming to Tokyo’s Pikachu Sweets by Pokémon Cafe next month. Not to be confused with the full-scale, sit-down Pokémon Cafe near Tokyo Station , Pikachu Sweets is a dessert stand located inside the Sunshine City shopping/entertainment complex in Tokyo’s Ikebukuro neighborhood. Seen in these photos is the Poké-patissiers’ newest creation, the Pikachu Shortcake Sandwich , made of two Pikachu-shaped slices of moist, fluffy shortcake with whipped cream and sliced strawberries between them , giving you a mix of sweet, tart, and milky flavors. Served in a little celebratory paper holder, this is a shortcake you can eat without your hands without getting your fingers messy , and the raised corners of the holder should keep the cake securely in place as you raise it up to snap a photo before your first bite, maybe with the Pikachu Sweets storefront in the background. Coming to the menu on the same day as the Pikachu Shortcake Sandwich is a new dessert drink, the Eevee Chocolate Frappe , with an adorable Eevee Pokémon 30th anniversary cookie and a swirl of whipped cream sitting atop the slushy chocolate drink , creating a color pattern evocative of Eevee’s coat. If you order a Pikachu Shortcake Sandwich plus an Eevee Chocolate Frappe or a Catch ‘Em Latte (“Get Latte” in Japanese) also gets you one of three 30th anniversary stickers with an illustration of a Pikachu wearing a cafe uniform. The lattes come in four different varieties (caffe latte, tea latte, caffe mocha, or caramel latte), hot or cold, and they’ll also be getting 30th anniversary foam art . The lineup goes on sale November 5 and will be available until December 31 , with both the Pikachu cake and Eevee frappe priced at 1,200 yen (US$7.60). Pikachu Sweets has no actual eat-in space, so customers generally either take their treats home or enjoy them on one of the benches within Sunshine City or in the adjacent outdoor plaza. The shop does caution, though, that because of the whipped cream, the Pikachu Shortcake Sandwich won’t keep for very long once it’s taken out of its refrigerated showcase, so they advise against waiting until you get home to eat it, especially since the store doesn’t provide cool packs to keep the cake chilled, and so this is a case where the healthiest thing to do is not resist digging into your dessert promptly after you have it in your hands. title: Super Mario creator Shigeru Miyamoto to receive Order of Culture from Japanese emperor
summary: If anyone deserves an Order of Culture, it’s-a-him. Every year, the Japanese holiday of Culture Day is observed on 3 November. This is also the day that the Emperor of Japan bestows the Order of Culture on selected citizens who made significant contributions to Japanese culture. These include researchers, leaders of industry, artists, doctors, and […]
details: If anyone deserves an Order of Culture, it’s-a-him . Every year, the Japanese holiday of Culture Day is observed on 3 November. This is also the day that the Emperor of Japan bestows the Order of Culture on selected citizens who made significant contributions to Japanese culture . These include researchers, leaders of industry, artists, doctors, and more. And when it comes to people who made an impact on Japanese culture, I doubt there’s anyone who’d disagree that Shigeru Miyamoto belongs in that group. After creating one of the most influential games of its time, Donkey Kong , in 1983, he played a critical role in revitalizing the slumping global video game industry with Japan at its center through Super Mario Bros. in 1985, creating both a revolutionary style of game and iconic characters that would thrive for the next 40 years. And everything he’s done since then, such as contributions to classic franchises like Zelda , Mario Kart , Star Fox and Pikmin, is just a ton of thick, sweet icing on the cake. In honor of this, Miyamoto will be presented the award by Emperor Naruhito at the Imperial Palace alongside seven other recipients , including Kenso Soai, who also won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry this year, and Shunichi Tokura, the composer of Pink Lady’s smash hit “UFO” and the current chair of JASRAC . In a press conference following the announcement, Miyamoto said, “I am truly happy to have found video games. As a creator, I have just as much fun developing games as the players do playing them. It is a joy to be able to keep doing this.” He also had the following advice for younger game designers: “I often tell them it is better not to start with a game they’re already a big fan of and find entertaining and just try to tweak it to make it ‘more fun.’ Instead of refining something that already exists, it is much more rewarding to start at the core and ask yourself, ‘Wouldn’t it be interesting if I tried this?’ Then focus your energy on building something from that idea.” Miyamoto will also be the first person from the gaming industry to have received this honor. After the news broke, there was an outpouring of support and congratulations from people all over Japan in online comments. “It’s long overdue, but wonderful news. Mario and Zelda are beloved not just in Japan but all over the world.” “I make recipes but was happy to hear he feels the same joy in his work and always thinks ‘Wouldn’t this be interesting?’ like I do.” “Even as the game market has grown to a huge scale, Mario and Zelda continue to rank among the top-sellers. He is a person who shaped countless lives all over the world.” “His work influenced our youths, the way we spent time with our family, and some of our unforgettable memories.” “Miyamoto never pandered to trends and always asked himself if his creations made people feel something.” “When he started out, video games were seen negatively. Now, his characters have appeared at the Olympics !” “I remember being completely hooked on Donkey Kong. I tried the famous shortcut trick over and over but could never do it!” “Paul McCartney even asked for Miyamoto’s autograph when they met and greeted him by singing the Super Mario song.” Speaking of Paul McCartney, it’d probably be fair to say that the next person from the game industry who should get an Order of Culture is none other than Koji Kondo, whose scores for Super Mario Bros. and Zelda were just as impactful and enduring as the games themselves. title: Tokusatsu hero “Moonlight Mask’s” pocket change donations help traffic accidents victims in Japan
summary: Small change and a big heart. A fun and really sweet aspect of Japanese culture is the trend of anonymous donations made in the name of masked people. Easily, the most iconic of these is Tiger Mask, a title taken by several people donating expensive randosel school bags to orphans and needy families and helping […]
details: Small change and a big heart . A fun and really sweet aspect of Japanese culture is the trend of anonymous donations made in the name of masked people. Easily, the most iconic of these is Tiger Mask , a title taken by several people donating expensive randosel school bags to orphans and needy families and helping out in other ways. Based on a wrestling manga hero of the same name, these real-life heroes have also led to a variety of copycats and spin-offs. I think there was even a kind-hearted Jason Mask one time. And every New Year’s Eve since 1974, on Sado Island in Niigata Prefecture, police have discovered a bag full of coins at one of their stations and outposts, along with a note that reads, “These are coins I collected, one by one every day. I’d be happy if it can help those suffering due to traffic accidents, even if just a little,” and is signed “Gekko Kamen,” meaning “Moonlight Mask” in English and also occasionally localized as “Moonbeam Man.” Hardcore tokusatsu fans will likely know one or more of these names as the precursor to the entire genre of superhero kids TV shows. Originally airing in the ’50s, Moonlight Mask was the archetypal masked, motorcycle-riding crusader of justice. Every year the police honor Moonlight Mask’s wishes and donate the coins to funds supporting those orphaned by traffic accidents. However, very recently, something truly unexpected happened. On 19 October, in Niigata City on the mainland of the prefecture, a police officer approached his patrol car and found an envelope on the windshield. Inside were coins totaling 240 yen (US$1.53) , and on the envelope a note said, “I’d be happy if it can help those suffering due to traffic accidents, even if just a little.” On the same day, about 1.5 kilometers from the first incident, another envelope was found at a police box in the Shirone Chuo area of the city. This one contained 299 yen (US$1.99) in change and had a note with the very same legendary words of Moonlight Mask. In both cases, no witnesses spotted anyone leaving the envelopes. This would mark the first time in over 50 years that Moonlight Mask or someone else using the same moniker donated to victims of car accidents outside of Sado Island. ▼ News report showing the envelopes and coins Deputy Chief Ryo Takahashi of the Niigata Minami Police Precinct said they will honor Moonlight Mask’s wishes and forward the 539 yen to children orphaned by traffic accidents. He added, “I am deeply moved by this person’s unending concern for the victims of car accidents. Because they are a hero, we are not investigating to uncover their true identity.” We can probably all agree that a noble deed should be respected regardless of its magnitude. However, this particular magnitude wasn’t enough to cover a combo at McDonald’s, and some readers of the news online had trouble fully coming to terms with that. “Oh… Well…” “I thought the report just had a typo in the number.” “It is the thought that counts, I guess…” “It’s always been New Year’s Eve. So why now?” “He does donate often. I looked it up, and this is his 53rd donation. Last time he gave 30,010 yen.” “I guess the rising cost of living is even putting a strain on Moonlight Mask.” “I wonder if this person is extremely poor themself.” “I want to say the amount isn’t important, but at a certain point wouldn’t this be considered a form of harassment?” “Only a horrible person would laugh at a gesture like this.” “This person must be pretty old by now. That was probably a good amount of money in their day.” “Their handwriting is very neat. They must be very meticulous.” “539 was the license plate number of Moonlight Mask’s motorcycle! Do your homework before shooting off your mouths!!!” That last comment would have been a cool detail, but a fun fact is that Moonlight Mask’s motorcycle had the license plate number Mu-8323 or 8328. Though it can be hard to see with from the angles the TV series’ scenes were filmed at, and with 1950s-quality cameras, some eagle-eyed fans were able to catch a peek of the superhero’s road-legal bike and at least narrow it down to those two. It’s especially ironic because while within the series private detective Juro Iwai is heavily implied to be Moonlight Mask’s secret identity, this is never confirmed, and even the actor for Moonlight Mask is listed as “?” in the credits. But anyone even remotely inclined to find out who he is need only look at the back of his bike and run a check on it. It just goes to show that the true spirit of Moonlight Mask is to help those in need and right the wrongs of society at all costs, even if your plan isn’t all that well thought out. details: Multiyear relationship will include new works specially created for L.A. audiences . At the age of 75 and with a career that’s already spanned more than 50 years, it wouldn’t be unnatural for Joe Hisaishi to be easing into retirement. Or maybe it would be, since the acclaimed composer best known for creating the soundtracks to Studio Ghibli’s most beloved anime films, including My Neighbor Totoro , Princess Mononoke , and Spirited Away , since Hisaishi continues to display a boundless passion and enthusiasm for making music and sharing it with as wide an audience as possible. For example, en route to setting a couple of Guinness World Records , he held a series of concerts at the Hollywood Bowl in Los Angeles over three days this past July. If you missed your chance to see him then, don’t worry, because Hisaishi has now been named Composer-in-Residence of the Los Angeles Philharmonic orchestra . This isn’t some simple honorary title/goodwill ambassador deal either. The L.A. Phil is describing the relationship as “a five-year creative partnership” that will start with the upcoming 2027/2028 concert season . In addition to recurring performances at all three of the organization’s customary venues (the iconic hillside Hollywood Bowl, the adjacent John Anson Ford Amphitheatre, and the downtown Walt Disney Concert Hall), Hisaishi “ will create new works specifically for the LA Phil and its audiences ” while also engaging in new commissions, recording projects, and educational and community outreach endeavors. “Los Angeles holds a special place in my musical life-from the premiere of my Harp Concerto with the LA Phil’s Emmanuel Ceysson at Walt Disney Concert Hall to our recent performances at the Hollywood Bowl and The Ford,” said Hisaishi following the announcement, and also that he’s “deeply honored” to be chosen for the role. “In the seasons ahead, I look forward to exploring new musical horizons with this extraordinary orchestra and sharing the spirit of discovery with audiences in Los Angeles and beyond.” ▼ An audio clip of one of Hisaishi’s previous Hollywood Bowl concerts View this post on Instagram ▼ With Hisaishi scheduled to be spending a lot more time in L.A., he’ll also be able to check out America’s first One Piece store , should the mood strike him. Hisaishi’s resume isn’t composed entirely of Ghibli soundtracks, as he’s also made contributed selected compositions or arrangements to other anime including Mobile Suit Gundam , Children of the Sea , Kimagure Orange Road , and Creamy Mami , as well as creating the soundtrack for video game Ni no Kuni and a handful of live-action Beat Takeshi movies. There’s no denying, though, that Hisaishi is most strongly associated with the work he’s done for Ghibli, As a matter of fact, there’s never been a Hayao Miyazaki-directed Ghibli feature film that Hisaishi didn’t write the score for, and with the studio’s track record of leaving a deep impression on fans around the world with its soundscapes, no doubt the new creative journey Hisaishi is about to embark on will be another movingly memorable one. details: Mr. Sato’s determination pays off in treat for the eyes and taste buds . Recently, our ace reporter Mr. Sato told us that he needed to go to Toranomon Hills , a shopping and entertainment complex in downtown Tokyo’s Toranomon neighborhood . Why? To eat ice cream. As Mr. Sato explained, recently he’s been seeing photo after photo of the soft serve ice cream from Dolce Tacubo , a dessert cafe located in Toranomon Hills, that’s been going viral. “Once the algorithm decides ‘You like this kind of stuff, don’t you?’ and starts filling your social feeds with it, you end up wanting to try it more and more, right?” he told us while heading out the door. Honestly, we’ve never known Mr. Sato to need any prodding by outside forces to convince him to eat ice cream, but we trust his savvy sense when it comes to photogenic sweets, and we anxiously awaited his report…which almost didn’t come in. Like a lot of Japanese shopping centers, Toranomon Hills has a food section, called T-Market , in its basement area. Mr. Sato assumed that’s where he’d find Dolce Tacubo, but after making multiple laps of the place, he still couldn’t find the cafe . So next he took the elevator up to the higher levels of the building, but he still couldn’t find it. Even consulting Google Maps didn’t clear things up, since the app told him to exit the building entirely, then come back in through another entrance, which didn’t make any logical sense to him. Eventually, it was human intelligence that put him on the right path, as Mr. Sato asked the Toranomon Hills employee posted at the taxi stand where he could find Dolce Tacubo, and they informed him that the cafe really is the T-Market zone, on basement level 2 , so back down the escalator our reporter went. At the risk of offending the sensibilities of interior designers with a penchant for minimalism, T-Market’s aesthetics might be a little too elegant for their own good. A number of the understated storefronts don’t have the shop’s name prominently displayed above their entrances, which is how Mr. Sato managed to walk right past this place multiple times … … before he finally realized this actually is Dolce Tacubo! He’d been almost ready to give up and go home before he spotted the surprisingly unassuming sign for Dolce Tacubo’s soft serve, but now that he knew he was in the right place, it was time to try the viral-hit dessert for himself. The ice cream is available in three varieties, vanilla, kabocha/Japanese pumpkin, and “mixed,” which gives you both flavors together. The vanilla is 1,000 yen (US$6.30) and the kabocha 1,200, which are premium prices for ice cream in Japan, and it’s a little weird that the mixed cone is 1,300 yen, more expensive than an all-kabocha cone despite half of it being the less-expensive vanilla ice cream. But hey, desserts aren’t always logical, so Mr. Sato decided to splurge on a mixed cone, and waited in the café’s eat-in space while the staff prepared his treat. It was every bit as beautiful as he’d hoped it would be . Amazingly, the swirly ridges of vanilla and kabocha wound through and wrapped around each other without any smearing save for a small section at the very top. The roasted pumpkin seeds are a classy touch too, and there’s so much care put into the presentation that it almost feels like personal pampering, putting a big smile on Mr. Sato’s face. Dolce Tacubo’s soft serve is more than just a proverbial pretty face, too . Both of the types of ice cream are rich and flavorful. If you’ve never had kabocha sweets before, they tend to be both lighter and sweeter than what you’d get with Western-style pumpkin pie, and this is an outstanding example of how well it can work as an ice cream flavor. In terms of texture Dolce Tacubo’s soft serve is actually on the firmer end of the spectrum within the category, dense enough that you can easily stand a spoon in it when it’s just-served. It melts easily on the palate, though, and has a silky mouthfeel without any significant grittiness. Mr. Sato can’t finish his taste-testing notes without mentioning the waffle cone too . It’s got a nice, substantial weight to it and a stimulating crunchiness that makes for some great synergy with the smooth ice cream. Beautiful, delicious, and interesting, Dolce Tacubo’s soft serve is a high-quality dessert by any metric, and Mr. Sato feels it definitely justifies not only its cost, but also the determination it might take to find it. details: And one more cooking hack will make your dashimaki tamago fluffier still . In terms of ingredients, dashimaki tamago is an incredibly simple dish. A type of Japanese omelet , you can make it with just three ingredients: eggs, water, and dashi (a stock made from fish and kelp that’s found in all sorts of Japanese dishes). The cooking process is also pretty straightforward, or maybe paradoxically straightforward, since dashimaki tamago is basically an omelet that you wrap ( maku ) back over itself multiple times, using a rectangular frying pan if you want the traditional squared-off shape. But just because dashimaki tamago is simple doesn’t mean it’s easy to make. The process can be surprisingly delicate, and while anyone with minimal cooking skills will be able to make dashimaki tamago that’s edible, it takes a deft hand to make dashimaki tamago with a wonderfully fluffy texture throughout its layers . So when we heard rumors of an unexpected ingredient substitution that’s supposed to make dashimaki tamago extra fluffy, we were all attentive ears and growling stomachs. First, let’s run through the basics of how to make dashimaki tamago . You’ll need: ● 3 eggs ● 1 tablespoon of dashi (we used the type called shirodashi) ● 3 tablespoons of water Mix them all up in a bowl, and also heat up an oiled frying pan on medium heat. Pour 1/3 of the mixture into the pan, give it a little mix with cooking chopsticks, and once it’s half-cooked, roll it to the front half of the pan. Reoil the now vacant part of the pan, add half of the ingredient mixture, and repeat the cooking and rolling process, then do it all again for the remainder of the mixture. So what’s the cooking hack substitution we’re trying today? Using sparkling/carbonated water instead of regular water . We heard about this idea through Asahi TV’s news/talk program Tantei! Knight Scoop , and then our reporter Natsuki Gojo headed into the SoraKitchen to test it out. Aside from the water swap, there’s only one other change to make, which is that when using the sparkling water, you mix the egg and dashi together first, and then add in the sparkling water right before cooking . OK, let’s see if this sparkling water swap really is such a bright idea! ▼ Regular water (left) and sparkling water (right) Starting with how the mixture of the three ingredients looked prior to cooking, as you can see in the above photo there’s a noticeable amount of fizz introduced by the sparkling water…at least initially . After stirring, though, the bubbles died down, and the regular and sparkling mixtures were equally calm. Once Natsuki poured them into the pan, though, the bubbles came back to the sparkling mix in a big way . Once both dashimaki tamago were done cooking, we laid them out side by side on a plate, and sure enough, the sparkling version had cooked up bigger and plumper, despite both versions having the exact same volume of ingredients . Next we sliced off a piece from each to examine their cross-sections, and were happy to see that the sparkling water substitution had produced exactly the sort of results we’d been hoping for! The regular-water version had congealed towards the bottom of the roll, but the sparkling dashimaki tamago had maintained a nice network of little air pockets while cooking, and those had made it fluffier. It wasn’t just the texture that had been enhanced, either. The sparkling dashimaki tamago was juicier too . Emboldened by this success, Natsuki decided to whip up one more batch of dashimaki tamago to test out another rumor she’d heard for further fluffiness . This time, instead of using three tablespoons of sparkling water, she used 175 milliliters (5.9 ounces), or roughly 10 tablespoons. Unsurprisingly, this resulted in even more bubbles at the pre-mix and cooking stages, and Natsuki found herself worried that the mixture might be too watery to cook up properly. But those fears turned out to be unnecessary, and this high-volume sparkling water version was the fluffiest and juiciest of all three she cooked . ▼ Sparkling water dashimaki tamago (left) and high-volume sparkling water dashimaki tamago (right) Natsuki herself is quick to point out that she doesn’t have a ton of experience cooking her own dashimaki tamago, so we’re not saying that using sparkling water is a must for good results. At the same time, her relative inexperience proves that you don’t have to be an expert to benefit from this simple ingredient swap, so if you’re looking to make your Japanese-style omelets as fluffy as you can, this is definitely worth giving a shot. title: This curry restaurant might have the worst location in Tokyo…or maybe the best
summary: Alk Road finds a way to turn a negative into a positive. Diners are so satisfied that they’ve made Alk Road one of […]
details: Alk Road finds a way to turn a negative into a positive . There are a lot of curry restaurants to choose from in Tokyo , but Spice Curry Alk Road stands out from many of its rice-and-roux rivals by virtue of its outstanding customer reviews. Diners are so satisfied that they’ve made Alk Road one of the top 100 curry restaurants in Tokyo based on average review scores on Tabelog, Japan’s most popular user-submitted restaurant site. Alk Road is just a one-minute walk from Iidabashi Station , so you could say that it has a great location…but as we found out on our visit, you could also make an argument that it has the worst location for a curry restaurant in Tokyo. If you head to the restaurant’s address, you’ll find yourself in front of this building. And yes, you will see the word “curry,” written in Japanese as カレー, on the signage . But the writing in front of “curry,” 上等? They’re the characters for “Joto,” as in “Joto Curry,” a curry restaurant chain that is not the independent Alk Road . So if you were to amble up here, you might think that Alk Road has gone out of business and been replaced by a Joto branch. A restaurant closing down and then a different one with the same specialty moving into the same spot isn’t all that unusual in Japan, since it lowers the renovation costs that you might have with, say, converting a yakiniku restaurant into a conveyor belt sushi joint. However, if you look down at the entrance to Joto Curry, you’ll see that Alk Road’s name is written next to the door … … and both Joto Curry’s and Alk Road’s names are written on the noren (cloth banner) hung above the entrance . Things get even more confusing when you step inside, since the first floor is clearly a Joto Curry branch. If you want to find Alk Road, what you have to do is turn to your right… …and follow the arrows pointing you up the stairs to the second floor… …and then, finally, you’ll have arrived at Alk Road! View this post on Instagram Yes, Alk Road has the confusing misfortune of being a curry restaurant that you can only access by first passing part-way through a different curry restaurant, and one that’s part of a famous chain to boot . This might seem like a recipe for constant animosity between the upstairs/downstairs neighbors, but it turns out that Joto Curry and Alk Road aren’t exactly direct competitors . Whereas Joto’s specialty is Japanese-style curry, Alk Road’s focus is on Indian-style curry, which the second-floor restaurant’s chef makes from scratch every day. While they’re both variations on the same basic concept (curry and rice), they use different kinds of roux, and different kinds of rice too – long-grain Indian rice for Alkroad’s curry, and short-grain Japanese rice for Joto Curry’s. So among diners in Japan, these two restaurants’ offerings are scratching different culinary itches, and even if you are in a perfectly 50-50 mood as to which type of curry they were craving, Alk Road actually offers a way to enjoy both in the same meal . One of Alk Road’s menu items is the Special Combination , a plate of curry rice in which one half is Joto’s roux and a pork cutlet, and the other is your choice of one of Alk Road’s house-specialty spice curries. ▼ Our 1,400-yen (US$8.80) Special Combination of Johto katsu curry and Alk Road chicken spice curry You also choose between Indian and Japanese rice for the Special Combination. We asked for the Indian rice, which made for a unique mixture of flavors and textures when paired with the Japanese roux. Both curries were excellent on their own, with Alk Road’s giving us a complex mixture of spices and seasonings and Joto’s being a more straightforward spiciness with a hint of sweetness in its flavor profile, and at the center of the plate where it flowed into one another we got yet another intriguingly fresh flavor. Should you want even more variety, Alk Road’s counter has an array of spices that you can shake onto your curry at your discretion, such as Cayenne pepper, roasted cumin, garam masala, and ajwain chili powder. This one-of-a-kind collaborative curry combination is something that’s only possible by nature of having two different curry restaurants operating so close to one another, and through it Alk Road has cleverly turned a negative aspect of its location into a positive. So while the search for Alk Road might be a little confusing, it’s well worth going to the trouble to find, just like with a certain soft serve ice cream specialist elsewhere in Tokyo . title: Baum vending machine in a Yokohama station lets us eat cake served on a luxury cruise ship
summary: Our favorite kind wasn’t even the one we expected, but they were all the baum-dot-com. details: Our favorite kind wasn’t even the one we expected, but they were all the baum-dot-com. It takes a lot to surprise us when it comes to Japanese vending machines , considering we’ve seen everything from Sriracha to sushi meals being sold in them. While the latter might sound a bit dubious, we’ve had relatively good results with the weird and wacky, and we’re always keeping our eyes peeled for new discoveries. The latest unusual vending machine we spotted was right outside of the ticket gates at Bashamichi Station on Yokohama’s Minatomirai Line . It was actually attracting a lot of curious glances from passersby, most likely because it was filled with Baumkuchen , the German spit cake that’s incredibly popular in Japan and usually goes by just “baum.” ▼ Cake from a vending machine somehow feels a lot safer than sushi. A closer look at the sign revealed that this particular baum was produced by Cocotomo Farm , which makes a 100-percent gluten-free cake using homemade rice flour from Aichi Prefecture. According to the sign, its brown rice-based hard baum is even given as a welcome gift on the luxury Asuka III cruise ship –Japan’s largest passenger ship–and was being sold in this machine at a discounted price to reduce food waste. Apparently there’s an Asuka III Meets 47 Prefectures Project , and this brand was selected as a representative for the Aichi Prefecture Room. As for why it’s being sold at this particular nondescript station in Yokohama, well, that part’s still a mystery–but perhaps it’s because there are several international cruise ship terminals in the area. There were plenty of baum options in the vending machine, but none of the selections were for the brown rice-based hard baum variety alone. Therefore, we opted for a combo pack with a slice of that one along with a slice of the white rice-based soft baum for 650 yen (US$4.14) , as well as a pack of hard baum edges for 500 yen. ▼ The machine takes cash or a variety of payment apps. All of the baum in this machine are frozen to preserve their freshness, so our prizes were quite chilly when they first came out. Luckily, the weather was relatively warm on this particular day, and the slices of cake had thawed out well by the time we got home. Here they were in their simple, unpretentious packaging. We were journalistically obligated to then immediately sample the slices of the soft and hard varieties, which were individually packaged. ▼ Soft baum (top) and hard baum (bottom) The soft baum was true to its name and had a refined, moist texture. We would have never known that it was gluten-free if the packaging didn’t alert us. Meanwhile, the hard baum had the exact opposite kind of feel. It was densely packed and required some force to bite down on, being chewy at the same time. It also carried the distinctive almost nut-like flavor of brown rice. We had always assumed that all baum tasted more or less the same, but this sampling threw that notion far out the window. Next, we broke out the hard baum edges. There were six individual pieces of slightly varying sizes packed into one bag. The hard baum edges were, if anything, even more densely packed with flavor and texture than the soft baum and regular hard baum alike. Sure, they were rough-looking on the outside, but they hid an intense surprise on the inside. In fact, they ended up being our favorite of the whole bunch. The value of six pieces for that price was also hard to beat. We have no idea how long the Cocotomo Farm vending machine is going to be stationed at Bashamichi Station–but we suppose that whenever it goes away, we’ll just have to get our baum fix from the ample varieties sold at at Muji instead . title: Visiting the “world’s most precarious temple” in China, where getting there is half the battle
summary: Xuankong Si is surprisingly both extremely out of the way and extremely crowded. details: Xuankong Si is surprisingly both extremely out of the way and extremely crowded. Our writer Seiji recently visited China, where he got a haircut on the side of the road and did some sightseeing. One of these sights was none other than Xuankong Si, or “The Hanging Temple” in English. Its name says it all really, in that it’s a temple clinging for dear life to the side of a sheer cliff. This temple is located in the Jinxia Gorge at the foot of Mt. Heng, known as one of China’s five great mountains. Of course, getting to a mystical temple like this was never meant to be easy and required Seiji to take a high-speed train from Beijing to Datong South Station, then drive from there into the mountains for about an hour. ▼ Seiji with his new haircut modeled after World Cup sensation Erling Haaland It was quite a haul, but Seiji was completely enamored with the Chinese countryside. The winding mountain roads reminded him perfectly of the area where Goku first met Bulma in Dragon Ball. There was a pulse of exotic adventure everywhere he looked. Little did he know, however, that his true battle still lay ahead. The visitor center leading into the temple area was far less mystical than other parts of his journey. The ticket counter opens at 7:30 a.m., and Seiji arrived at 8:40. However, he was told that the tickets had already sold out. As luck would have it, tickets are sold in two batches, with 600 in the morning and another 600 in the afternoon. This meant he’d have to wait until noon to try again. By 10 a.m., a significant lineup was already forming, and Seiji watched with amazement as it just got bigger… …and bigger… …and bigger… …and bigger with time. By noon, it looked exactly like the line to get into Comiket . It’s actually possible to book tickets in advance, but only for Chinese residents. This meant Seiji had no choice but to wait in line, but as he listened to two old ladies shouting at each other, he wondered why all these other people didn’t just make reservations. Luckily, this time he could get tickets. Two types are sold: a general admission to the area for 15 yuan (US$2.25) and access to the temple itself for 100 yuan ($15). Considering how much effort it took to get this far, there was no way he was going to skip entering The Hanging Temple. From this point, a bus ride was required, but it only took eight minutes and cost 20 yuan. But after all that traveling and waiting, he was happy to see that it was all worth it for this spectacular scenery. This temple was mentioned on Time Magazine’s Top 10 Precarious Buildings , and since it was the only temple on the list, Seiji figures it’s safe to call it the world’s most precarious temple. In this case, the word “precarious” doesn’t suggest poor construction or actual hazards, but a certain tilt that gives the feeling of precariousness. This place certainly had that feeling in spades. As he walked along narrow paths jutting out from sheer cliffs that seemed to tower over him, the ground spread out far, far below him. Seiji was never especially afraid of heights, but here he occasionally felt a little woozy and had to brace himself against the wall. This structure was around 1,500 years old, and as is often the case with older buildings, everything feels a little smaller than usual. The railings everywhere were only about waist-height, adding to a sense that he was walking through the air. ▼ No problem there. It truly felt like a temple in the sky, giving our writer a sensation he often felt during dreams where he was flying but then suddenly forgot how to fly and plummeted back to Earth. It was a one-of-a-kind experience and well-steeped in Chinese culture. Seiji felt a sense of awe beyond most other places he’s been in his life, and would highly recommend a visit to anyone. His only advice is to purchase the ticket to enter the temple, because it’d be a waste to travel all that way and not climb up to it. Also, make sure you arrive early because the lineup for tickets is no joke, and it’d be an even bigger waste to travel all that way and not even be able to get near Xuankong Si. summary: Sakura Oda สมาชิก Morning Musume '26 ที่จะจบการศึกษาหลังอยู่วงมา 15 ปี (คอนเสิร์ตอำลา 11 ธ.ค. ที่ Yokohama Arena) เผยในงานเปิดตัวโฟโต้บุ๊ก "Sakura" ว่าต้นสังกัดห้ามสมาชิกไปสระว่ายน้ำ ทะเล และออนเซ็นในวันหยุด เธอใส่ชุดว่ายน้ำแค่ตอนถ่ายงาน แต่ซื้อชุดว่ายน้ำของตัวเองไว้แล้ว เตรียมไปสระกับเพื่อนสมัยเด็กสัปดาห์แรกที่เป็นอิสระ และจะกินมาม่า ไก่ทอด เค้กที่โดนห้ามด้วย
details: Anime Una idol japonesa revela las insólitas prohibiciones de su grupo La cantante Sakura Oda se retirará en diciembre tras 15 años de carrera en el grupo. Kenji 24 de octubre de 2026 1 Comentarios ADS Ser una idol en la industria japonesa exige un nivel de disciplina que muchas veces roza lo absurdo. Durante la presentación de su último libro de fotografías titulado Sakura , la cantante Sakura Oda , integrante del legendario grupo Morning Musume. '26 , sorprendió a la prensa al revelar algunas de las restricciones más insólitas que tuvo que cumplir durante su vida privada en sus 15 años dentro de la agrupación. Durante el evento celebrado en Tokio con motivo del lanzamiento de su libro publicado por la editorial Wani Books, la artista compartió detalles sobre las estrictas normas que rigen la rutina diaria de las integrantes. Según explicó, la administración prohíbe rotundamente que las chicas visiten albercas, playas o baños termales en su tiempo libre. Aunque Oda lució trajes de baño en varias sesiones fotográficas oficiales a lo largo de su carrera, confesó que jamás ha podido usar uno en su vida cotidiana desde que ingresó al grupo, ya que las reglas no permiten exponerse en ese tipo de lugares públicos. Apasionada de la natación desde pequeña, la cantante ya tiene organizado su regreso a la vida cotidiana inmediatamente después de su concierto de despedida en el Yokohama Arena el próximo 11 de diciembre. Oda contó entre risas que ya compró su propio traje de baño y planea ir a una piscina con sus amigas de la infancia durante su primera semana de libertad. De igual forma, admitió que dedicará un día entero a romper su estricta dieta comiendo sopas instantáneas, pollo frito, chocolates, helados y pasteles, algo que tenía totalmente restringido debido al riguroso control de calorías y metabolismo que le exigían en su carrera. Mirando hacia el futuro, la artista expresó su deseo de seguir vinculada al mundo del entretenimiento a través del teatro y la actuación, dos facetas que le resultaba prácticamente imposible explorar debido a la exigente agenda del grupo musical. Con su salida oficial, la cantante espera tener el tiempo y la libertad necesarios para interactuar más de cerca con el público en esta nueva etapa profesional. Morning Musume es uno de los grupos de idols femeninas más influyentes e históricos de la cultura pop japonesa, formado originalmente en 1997 dentro del colectivo Hello! Project. A lo largo de casi tres décadas, la agrupación se ha mantenido vigente gracias a un sistema rotativo de graduaciones e incorporaciones de nuevas generaciones de jóvenes talentos. Dentro de este icónico proyecto musical, Sakura Oda se consolidó como una de las vocalistas principales y referentes indiscutibles desde su ingreso en 2012 como parte de la undécima generación. Su retiro este 11 de diciembre marcará el cierre definitivo de una trayectoria de 15 años dedicados al escenario. ¿Qué opinas sobre las estrictas reglas que deben cumplir las idols en su vida privada?
